The House resumed from Monday, February 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-109, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government is coming before us with Bill C-109 asking for Parliament to give the Government the authority to borrow $25 billion. We have debated this issue at this point in time for a total of four hours and forty-five minutes. That is a little less than $5 billion per hour. Frankly, when I look at the over-all thrust of government programs to date, or lack thereof, as a Canadian citizen who has been charged with the responsibility of representing my constituents, I do not think the Government has earned the right to be accorded this $25 billion.
There are many areas where the Government has not acted. Certainly one of the areas in recent times where we have seen a total lack of leadership has been in the Government's response to the Supreme Court judgment on the issue of abortion.
The federal Government instead of showing leadership on a very difficult issue has passed the problem to the provinces so that both the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) have allowed a chaotic situation to reign across the country because

March 1, 1988

they do not have the political courage to bring to the House of Commons some legislation to deal with this extremely sensitive issue for Canadians. That is one area where the Government is getting an F in its report card but there are many other areas.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel- Ahuntsic (Mrs. Killens) just pointed out the situation of the homeless. We have come out of the year of the homeless and what response have we had from the federal Government to deal with the killing issue for Canadians? Absolutely none. If anything, we have seen the Government divest itself of responsibility in the same way that it did with the Supreme Court judgment, namely, it passed it off to the provinces. We now have a situation where social housing in Canada is no longer under the leadership of the federal Government, but is passed off to the provinces. In fact, the only area where the federal Government has maintained sole jurisdiction has been in the area of co-operative and native housing where no kudos need to be given. This is another area where we have a total lack of leadership.
We heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) most recently lauding the fact that Canada is deemed to be the country among the OECD nations which has the largest growing economy for fiscal year 1987.

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Government Members are applauding. But what they fail to recognize is that at the same time we have these wonderful statistics coming from the mouth of the Minister of Finance, one in five Canadian children is living in poverty. In fact, we have a situation where thousands upon thousands of children are going to school hungry, and do not have homes. What kind of response have we had from this Government?
Under tax reform, the Government put one million poor people on the tax rolls for the first time in Canadian history- on the tax rolls, Madam Speaker. The Minister of Finance through the tax measures he has introduced since 1984 has brought onto the tax rolls one million people who were never paying taxes before. Now the Minister comes out with tax reform. He actually has the nerve to stand up in the House and beat his breast, saying he has taken 850,000 off the tax rolls. What he does not tell Canadians is that he and his Government were in a position to put one million new people on the tax rolls.

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What about all the new jobs that people have?

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Now there are 850,000 people taken off the tax rolls. That is Tory tax reform. Take from the poor and hand out to the rich.
In our Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare, we tried to have the issue of child poverty addressed as a priority. In fact, the child poverty action group implored us to do so. The Canadian Council on Social Development and the National Council on Welfare asked us to bring forward
Borrowing Authority
this issue as a priority issue. Instead, the committee on health and welfare has chosen to study mechanisms for financing health care, including trips to the United Kingdom, Sweden, the Netherlands and I think Germany. We are taking a world tour to study health care when we should be looking at the question of Canadian children who are going to school hungry and are without roofs over their heads. In 1988 in an economy as vibrant as the Canadian economy the situation is a national disgrace and a national tragedy. How does the Government expect us to pass a blank cheque for $25 billion when it does not have the heart to care about the children in our country who are going hungry?
When the Minister of Finance is asked questions in the House about what he is doing with social policy, he just parrots OECD statistics, which do not mean a lot when you do not have bread on the table or a roof over your head.
I would like to spend a moment dealing with a much more personal issue to me. Over the years we hear many difficult and sad stories, we hear many stories that would break your heart. I had the occasion about two months ago to hear directly from a woman who did not live in my riding. She lived in a neighbouring community but had not gotten a response from her local M.P. so came to see me. She came because her son who was 17 years of age, a model student, a model volunteer, the kind of son any parent would love to have, had died. He had died after eating an apple turnover at an Arby's restaurant. The reason he died is that apple turnovers, unbeknownst to the young man, contained ground up hazel nuts, nuts so small they cannot be seen by the human eye. This young man had eaten apple turnovers at other restaurants. He had eaten them at McDonald's and at Harvey's. He assumed that an apple turnover is what it says, an apple turnover. He did not think an apple turnover was an apple and a nut turnover. He knew he had an allergy. As soon as he ate this apple turnover he started to have a reaction. He had been told by his physician that if he ever underwent an attack, which in the medical jargon is called a reaction of anaphylactic shock, that he would have time to get to the hospital. His mother told me this story. He jumped on his bicycle and pedalled home. He got in the front door and was barely speaking at that point. He was choking and losing consciousness. He asked his father for help. His mother told me that she did not even have time to say goodbye to her son because he was dead before she even had a chance to wake up. She told me that she could sue the company involved, but she does not want to do that because to sue the company will not bring her son Christian back. She said that she would like the Government to do something to prevent this kind of tragedy from happening to another young person.
This occurred in December. In my naivety, I believed that there are many issues that one comes across in political life, some of which are partisan and some of which are not. I felt that this was not a partisan issue. I felt that this was an issue

March 1, 1988
Borrowing Authority
with which any parent could identify. Unfortunately, when the food and drug regulations were brought in this issue was omitted. It is not a sin of commission but of omission.
In the 1960s when food and drug regulations were brought in, the Government felt that when people went to grocery stores, they should be able to know what they were eating. They should be able to pick up a can of soup and read the ingredients on the label. We know that now, in 1988, the Canadian appetite for food is changing rapidly. We know that many Canadians eat out more often than they eat in their own homes. Why have the food and drug regulations not kept pace with the times? Why have the food and drug regulations not reflected the fact that most people do not always cook their meals at home? Many people are often forced to eat on the run, and it is not practical in 1988 to tell a person with an allergy that the only way to deal with that allergy is to eat at home.
I thought that I would speak to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) privately and tell him that there is obviously a loophole in the law. As I did more investigation, and I had some tremendous help, support and information from the Canadian Allergy Information Association and the president of that association, Mrs. Susan Daglish, I became aware of the fact that approximately one person in Canada dies every month as a result of an allergic reaction. We do not know how many more end up in hospital or how many more have unreported seizures, because that type of data is not collected.
I do know that I told the Minister that there seems to be a loophole in the law. I said that if we could get an agreement, perhaps changes could be brought in. I did not want to make this a political issue. I would rather have the Minister bring forward amendments to the Food and Drugs Act which would include labelling of fast foods, as a start. I recognized that this would not be an easy solution or a quick-fix. It would not save every life, because in some cases there are other impinging factors. However, it seemed to me to be a reasonable request.
In this day and age when companies are spending thousands and in some cases probably millions of dollars on fancy packaging and gimmicks to catch the eye of the consumer, at the very least Canadian consumers should have the right to know what it is they are eating. When Canadians go out to get an apple turnover or a hamburger, whether it is called a Whopper, a Big Mac or whatever, it would be nice for them to know what they are eating. Since that right was accorded to us for groceries back in the 1960s, and we know that today fast food is much more prevalent, why can we not have the same right when we go out to eat in restaurants?
I was a little naive. When I raised the matter with the Minister, he said he would look into it. I did not hear anything further for a month or so, so I decided, in order to stimulate the discussion, that I would bring forward a resolution. In fact,
I raised the issue with the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare. I must say that the response of the Chairman, the
Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), who has a medical background himself, was most encouraging.
Conservative members of the committee agreed with me that something should be done about food labelling and, in fact, they summoned the Minister to come before the committee to explain why there is no requirement for labelling of fast food at the moment. What we heard was a litany of excuses longer than the menus at most fast-food restaurants. The Minister said he could not do it because some restaurants sell hamburgers and hot dogs in the same packages and, God forbid, some restaurants may use peanut oil when cooking. It was a response from a Minister who had made up his mind that he would not go ahead with this and who then needed to summon all his arguments as to why he could not. It was not the response of a Minister who should be showing leadership and telling his Department that he wants this done and showing the vehicle to carry it out.
No one is suggesting that if we legislated labelling all of the problems would be solved tomorrow and all the labelling would be proper as of tomorrow. Obviously that is why we have regulations. That is why we permit the Government, in its wisdom, to come forward with Governor in Council decisions relating to issues like labelling. There may be exceptional cases or anomalies that cannot be encompassed in the legislation. That is why we tell the Minister that he has the discretion to come forward with a package which will meet the basic need of Canadians to know what they eat and still take into consideration the fact that at some point there may be matters that are not covered by the legislation.
What I saw was a Minister who was simply prepared to come before the committee to give us a bunch of excuses and to even go so far as to blame the families of the victims, to blame people who died because there is no labelling on fast foods or restaurant foods; the victim did not know that in the case of an Arby's turnover, for example, there are hazelnuts ground up so fine that the eye cannot see them.
The Minister even had the audacity to suggest that people who have severe allergic reactions should consider not eating out. In this day and age the Minister should not be giving reasons and excuses, he should be coming forward with legislation to deal with the problem.
Certainly the members of the Health and Welfare Committee did agree that we should move with legislation on this. I am very sorry that instead of accepting the view of all the members of that committee, including the chairman who has a medical background, the Minister was merely there to provide excuses. Now he along with the rest of his Government is asking for $25 billion to carry out the programs of Government. He is asking for the authority to borrow money to permit the Government to carry on with its other functions. I say that in order for the Government to be accorded borrowing authority, it has to display some sense of responsibility.
In the case of the fast-food labelling issue, the Minister has not displayed responsibility, caring and concern for Canadians,
March 1, 1988

but merely a shallow, knee-jerk response, a litany of excuses. Frankly, it was something that I did not expect, even from that Minister.
The proof is in the pudding. I received some information in a phone call this morning. I have not corroborated it totally, so I am passing it along only for information and edification. I heard that at least two major retail outlets in the fast-food business have now decided themselves that they intend to label their foods. As I understand it, they are moving not to label foods item by item but to label foods which have an allergic potential, and certainly that could be expanded.
Flow can we accept the excuses of the Minister of Health who as late as last week said that this could not be done, when the fast-food chains themselves are now moving in that direction? The Minister of National Health and Welfare is not supposed to be a spokesman for what cannot be done for the health of Canadians, but a spokesman for what can and should be done.
[DOT] (M30)
Surely it is not unreasonable in 1988 to suggest that when you go into a restaurant you should have the right to know what you are eating just as you do when you cook a meal in your own home. It is shameful that these major hamburger chains have found the wherewithal to act when, last week, the Minister of National Health and Welfare said it could not be done. It could not be done because he did not want it to be done.
In his litany of excuses he kept referring to the fact that, oh, there were two deaths? Why should we worry about that? It is not just one or two deaths. He said some people are seeking a quick fix. No doubt he was referring to me because I raised it by way of resolution and asked the committee to deal with it. He said it is too bad a couple of people have died but let us look at consumer responsibility. Yet the more you delve into this issue, the more you realize people are dying in a way which is completely preventable.
I read into the record the case of a man who died at a New Year's Eve party, I believe, in New Brunswick; the case of a Chatham couple whose daughter died as a result of an allergic reaction; there are cases in Quebec and across the country. Yet the Minister was more interested in a knee-jerk reaction, in protecting his own political backside than he was in actually dealing with the issue, putting the health of Canadians first and foremost, and giving them a chance to determine that what they eat is not going to kill them.
Is it such an unreasonable request to have the Minister take up his responsibility and inform Canadians that what they are eating is not going to kill them? That seems to me to be a primary responsibility of the Minister. If he is not there to prevent people from dying, what is he there for? He is there for excuses. He is there to find reasons why not.
Borrowing Authority
I believe the issue of food labelling has the support not only of Members on this side of the House but the support, spoken and unspoken, of many members on the government side. I suggest to the Government, and the Minister in particular, that if they want the Opposition to approve the spending of $25 billion of taxpayers' money on various programs, then they should start dealing with programs not currently available.
One program that I would insist the Government do its most to introduce in this session deals with the whole question of food labelling. It is not enough for the Minister to ask why. It is time for him to say why not, and when and where and how, and to get on with it and start taking his responsibilities seriously. We intend to continue to press the issue both in committee and in the House. I believe it has all-Party support and I will certainly be continuing to press the Government, in the context of Bill C-109 as well as any other government Bill, to deal with the health of Canadians which it is not at the moment.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to comment on the speech we just heard from the Hon. Member.
I will not ask her a question but I would not be surprised if she wishes to comment afterwards.
I noted her comments about food labelling and I am sure everyone wishes that we could clearly state what is in the food people eat in a restaurant. However, I do not think she has outlined the difficulties. As a government Member I would like to see something done if it is practical to do it. I was also pleased that the Hon. Member did not use this issue to try and destroy an industry, for partisan political purposes, like she did in the mussels affair in the fall of last year.
The primary reason I stood up to comment concerns the record of this Government. Some 1.1 million more people are working under this Government than under the previous Government. Some 85 per cent of those are working full-time compared to 85 per cent part-time under previous Governments. Some 500,000 fewer people are living below the poverty line. A lot of those people are children. That is a tremendous record. Some 800,000 people have been taken off the tax rolls. The child tax credit has been increased and is being paid at a time most advantageous to the parents, just before Christmas. Because interest rates have gone down, so have housing costs.
Surely the Hon. Member considers this a fantastic record compared to that of the Government formed by the Liberal Party to which she belongs?

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I could point out that over the 20-year history of Liberal Governments in Canada the average unemployment rate was 5.2 per cent, still far too high but a far cry from what we have at the moment. I do not think the Hon. Member should be bragging about current unemployment levels.
However, I would like to most strenuously object to the statement concerning my role as opposition health critic in relation to the poisoned mussels. It was the Minister of

March 1, 1988
Borrowing Authority
National Health and Welfare who, in a completely inept but opportune way, issued an over-all health warning for all shellfish without even knowing the difference between a bottom feeder and a crustacean. He completely misread and misunderstood his own portfolio. This led to a tremendous decrease in the sale of seafoods of all kinds. Frankly, if I had been sitting in his chair I never would have issued such a warning. It was completely without any basis and displayed his ignorance of the seafood problem.
The point I would most like to stress is that the Hon. Member has said he would like to see fast-food labelling. When you are the Minister undoubtedly you have to look at the difficulties you are going to encounter in labelling fast-food packaging. The whole point of my 20-minute speech was to say that it is not enough to say these are all the reasons why we cannot do it. When you are a Minister you say, department, I would like to have labelling of fast-foods and I want a report on my desk within the next two weeks to tell me how that can be accomplished. That is why we have regulations and Governor-in-Council decisions.
There may be some areas where it is not workable. We are all reasonable people. We are going to sit down and look at those areas. However, you start not from the premise of what cannot be done but what can be done and go from there to bring forward labelling regulations. We are looking at it right now with respect to drug labelling.
1 must give credit to a Private Member on the government side, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin), who introduced legislation governing the labelling of drugs. Now the Government is going to move in that direction. The Government has tabled its intentions and is now seeking responses from consumers and the industry. The whole process may take a year. No one is suggesting it is going to be done overnight. However, the Government is saying it is going to find out how it can be done.
On food labelling, the Minister comes before the committee and says we cannot do it and here are the reasons why. He does not say we can do it. What I am suggesting, and hopefully my friend who sat on that committee on an interim basis, and 1 am not sure if he is going to remain as a permanent member, and his colleagues will prevail upon the Minister to bring in some substantive legislation and indicate his intention to move in that direction. He should say they are prepared to look at working out all the details.
Perhaps all the packaging cannot be labelled in as complete a way as 1 would like, but let us start by establishing our bottom line, seeing how we are going to get to it as opposed to throwing up our hands and saying it is not possible because someone from the Opposition raised it and I am not going to have a knee-jerk reaction just because a couple of people died. That is what I object to and that is why I am not going to support this Bill.

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the thing which strikes me about this issue of allergies, fast-foods, and the tragic deaths which have resulted therefrom is that it should be possible to stand up in this Parliament and raise a very important health issue without being attacked for trying to undermine an industry. Obviously every Party in this House is concerned about employment. Some of us believe that we have more effective policies for achieving those objectives, but surely the principle is that people have a right to know what they are eating, particularly when dealing with large fast-food corporations such as McDonald's, Harvey's, and other corporations which make a profit from food which many nutritionists will tell us has very little nutritional value.
Since these corporations are making a profit surely they could live within some community standards. The purpose of this place is to identify priorities. When there are deaths in the community it is the responsibility of this place to respond and take some action. We will figure out the details and determine what is possible and what is not possible, but we start with that principle. I think it is a mistake for back bench Conservatives to get up and simply defend the record of the Government.
My colleague has said that he is in favour of action in this area. Let him follow the example of some of his colleagues who have recently objected to government policy in a public way. Let him show some leadership. This is a crucial issue which involves people's lives and those corporations can make adjustments.

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am glad the Member raised the issue of corporations because, as I said, I received word this morning that at least two major chains are moving in that direction. It is ironic that even the major corporations are prepared to move when the Government said it cannot be done. Obviously it can be done and it is up to the Minister to show some leadership. That is my intention in bringing the issue to the fore. I hope that other government Members who do support the legislation will put pressure on the Minister so that he will finally at least follow the lead that has already been established by some major fast-food chains.

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I used to have a lot of respect for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). I am very disappointed and 1 am going to read the record of the debate they had last week in committee.
I would like to add my own personal experience. I have a 25-year old son who is allergic to nuts. He is married. I am in Ottawa most of the time but my children have the key to the house. He came to the house alone-my husband was not there-and he went for the cookies. He ate about six or eight cookies. It was his mistake, it has nothing to do with going to a public place to eat. It was in my house. He should have been careful but the reaction set in. His face gets all swollen, his vocal cords tighten up and he can hardly speak.
March 1, 1988

He dialed the phone number of my daughter who is married and has a baby son. She was alone at home but understood that he was in trouble and that she had to do something quickly. She told him to crawl to the door and open it, that she would phone the neighbour to go and take him to the hospital. She did not want to dress her child in order to take him to the hospital. He was taken to the hospital and, luckily, survived.
I was so touched by the story of my colleague, the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), and I was so disappointed by the Minister's stand in committee last week. A strong Minister gives orders to his functionaries. In this case the Minister is being very weak. What does the Member for Hamilton East intend to do from now on in order to help people like my son?

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we are planning to continue the investigation in committee. We have made arrangements to hear from the Canadian Food Services Association and also from the Canadian Allergy Information Association. We are planning to pursue it and hopefully we can finally get the Minister on side.

subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the borrowing authority which the Government is seeking today for $25.3 billion raises the fundamental question of what the Government has done, what its performance has been. This question is raised by the simple fact that it is the prerogative of Parliament to approve monetary authority, spending authority, for the Government. The basis of parliamentary democracy is that the executive, the Crown, has to come before the people's representatives, the Commons, to ask for authority to spend money. The question raised by this borrowing authority is what is the record of the Government, what has it done, what have its policies been, and has it faced the issues of the day.
While it is often a mistake to respond to the remarks of a previous speaker and digress from your own prepared notes or the thoughts you had planned to bring to debate, today is an exception. The issue raised by my colleague with regard to the labelling of fast-foods in order that people who have allergies know what they are eating is an issue of the day which cuts to the core of the issue of borrowing authority, that is, the accountability of the Government to the people's representatives.
Over the last few weeks it has come to public attention that a person can go to a fast-food restaurant, eat food, and die as a result without having had any warning of this possible consequence. This has been broadcast by the media, people have approached their Members of Parliament, and the Commons has begun to speak. It is calling the executives to account, asking what it has done.
This priority requires action now. That it has emerged in the public spotlight only in the last few weeks is no excuse for inaction. Just because we call upon the Government to act speedily does not mean the action we are calling for is an
Borrowing Authority
ignorant, knee-jerk response to an onslaught of media attention. In fact, this is democracy at its best. The media has made an issue known and the Commons is bringing the issue forward and demanding that the executive take action rather than find excuses and be stuck in a morass of inaction.
I wanted to take the opportunity at the beginning of my remarks on this borrowing authority to echo the comments of my colleagues who said that it is time for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to ensure the labelling of food in fast-food restaurants as a priority and for him to tell his civil servants to bring forth a plan of action. He must put aside his behaviour which until now has been stalling, excuses, and responding to an industry lobby rather than to the needs of individual Canadians, the needs of young people who, because of the allergies from which they suffer, are playing Russian roulette with their lives every time they enter a fast-food restaurant. We require the food industry to label products in stores; surely we can also require that the fast-food industry label the foods which it makes available in restaurants.
That issue goes to the core of the whole question of borrowing authority. The Government, the executive, the frontbenchers, the power wielders, are coming before this humble Chamber to ask for authority to spend money. This is our opportunity to make the Government listen to the voice of the people and respond to their wishes. We must ask what it has done about the fundamental issues facing ordinary Canadians, when it asks for borrowing authority of $25 billion. For example, it has not yet acted with regard to labelling fast-foods for allergies. Hopefully, during this debate, some Members on the Government side will convince the Cabinet to take action in this area.
When we debate this Borrowing Authority Bill, we must begin by examining the Government's over-all budgetary policy. It recently introduced a rather slim Budget compared to previous budgets it introduced during its mandate. The most recent Budget outlined what the Government has done and what it would do in the future. Two of the initiatives the Government has taken in its Budget are tax increases. One of those tax increases is directly related to the Mulroney trade deal.

Madam Speaker, I will not argue with the Chair. We still know that this trade deal is part of the Budget. The revenue to the federal Government will decrease as a result of the trade agreement because tariffs will drop. At the same time, the Government is attempting to replace that decrease in revenue by raising taxes by some $500 million in the Budget. The Prime Minister, who is even less popular than a former unmentionable prime minister, brags about the so-called great future that he believes this deal will bring to Canada. Yet we are already beginning to see the cost of the deal in the form of increased taxes that are directly linked to this trade deal orchestrated by one of this country's most unpopular prime ministers who, of course, earned that unpopularity.
While the Government seeks this borrowing authority, we must ask what it has done with the money it has taken from Canadians. When one considers the budgets brought down by the Government since it was elected, we see that it has hit the middle class families hardest in terms of tax increases. The ordinary Canadian family has suffered under the Government's increased tax, while at the same time the Government promised tax relief. It states that everyone will receive a tax break on their income tax, but it has raised taxes to such an extent while it has been in office that any relief in taxes now will still leave a net tax increase, mostly for middle class families.
The Budget promised further cuts in the deficit and further cuts in spending. If the Government plans to fulfill those promises, if it is successful after the next election, it will have to cut family allowances and old age pensions in order to meet those budgetary targets. If it is re-elected, the Government will have to take away services that Canadians have come to value. Therefore, on the basis of its budgetary policies, this Parliament cannot approve the borrowing authority request of the Government.
We cannot approve of what the Government has done. The generation before us in the 1930's fought for changes in social policy and met the challenge of identifying and addressing the key issues of the day. The CCF, and the NDP which followed it, which included people like Stanley Knowles, Tommy Douglas and the others who worked with them, helped to bring about medicare, old age pensions and other programs. The generation before us met the critical challenge of identifying these issues and succeeded in bringing about program changes that might make this a better place to live.
What has the Government done to face the key challenges of our generation? What has it done about poverty? What has it done about the environment? What has the Government done about human survival in the nuclear arms race? What has it done about employment and justice for all? Those are the key issues which must be addressed. Those are the substantive issues. It is not simply a question of what is reported on the front page of The Globe and Mail or who is being interviewed on The Journal. It is not a question of where the media focus is today or next week. Those are some fundamental and societal issues that have to be addressed in our generation if we are to achieve what our previous generation achieved, that is making Canada a better place to live.
I put that challenge to the Government. What thinking is it doing in these areas in order to bring about real change? We all know that something like one-fifth of the Canadian population suffers from functional illiteracy. They cannot read or write well enough to hold down jobs or function in our society. I have met such individuals in my riding and in the process of signing up membership in my own Party. Through the simple process of meeting people in one's constituency, asking for their support and getting them to sign up as members of one's Party, when it comes to the last step of the process, I find they cannot write their names or that all they can write are their names, or they have to put an X which has to be witnessed. There are people in our community behind the statistics which indicate there are real needs that must be met. Functional illiteracy is part of this whole picture of poverty.
I know of a specific case of a woman in my riding who has spent many years struggling with some disabilities and with the need for training. She has yet to receive this training. I brought this matter to the attention of the Canada Employment and Immigration Department. I am hoping for some progress in this area.
Another critical area that illustrates the whole question of poverty in our country is that of our homeless. There are people living in Canada who do not have a roofs over their heads. It is really quite unimaginable that we live in a country where some people do not even have a place to sleep. I saw statistics in a recent book of the numbers who are homeless in the City of New York and the City of Toronto.
The Government has come before us to ask for the authority to borrow over $25 billion. This is the House of Commons. This is the place where we hold the executive accountable. This is the place in which the king must answer for his spending. Therefore, we ask what the Government has done. The answer is in its budgetary policy. It has hit the middle-class families. What has it done about the key issues of our generation, about poverty, the environment, nuclear arms and unemployment? There is silence when that question is put. The Government should get on with meeting the essential priorities of this nation. It should act on some of the immediate priorities, including the question of allergies, fast-food outlets and
March 1, 1988

the need for labelling. When the Government comes before this House it should be capable of saying it has taken action rather than responding to the question with silence.

Therefore, by hook or by crook, by every possible means, it will be kept under that. It is surely a confession of failure to have the deficit reach that amount.
On the other hand, the Government has failed in so many areas. The Hon. Member was dealing carefully with those various shortcomings, and the actions that the people need to be taken, which have not been taken. I wonder if the Hon. Member would take up this topic of failure of the Government, on its own assumptions, and the creative possibilities of meeting the needs of Canadians, using the borrowing power of the Government in that sense and perhaps finding $25 million quite acceptable, but doing it in a context in which we could get the country back to full employment, being able at full employment to balance the budget and reduce the deficit about which the Government is so worried. To achieve the prosperity and well-being of the Canadian people has always been our concern as New Democrats, even in the earlier days of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation, and to fulfil the vision that moved our founders who came to public life with the determination of the social gospel.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the interesting thing about the whole question of deficits and borrowing, more particularly about deficits, is that while parties of the Conservative persuasion, whether in Canada, the United States or in other countries, tend to talk about spending less, parties of the Social Democratic persuasion such as mine tend to talk about the worth-while expenditures which need to be made. But the thing that strikes me most of all is that even when a Government of the Conservative persuasion takes power, spending does not seem to go down. It spends for different things. Different people get tax breaks and different people get the benefit of the public treasury.
Borrowing Authority
I think right now of the Government's policy of tax reform in its last budget in which it continued its pattern of increasing taxes on the ordinary Canadian family. At the same time it continues the policy of failing to tax large corporations which are making hundreds of millions of dollars in profits. In other words, corporations which make a profit pay no taxes as a direct government policy. At the same time the Government raises the taxes on middle-class Canadian families. When push comes to shove, we know that when a Government comes into office and tells us it will not waste money, it will not spend unwisely, that it will be frugal, what it in fact does is simply shift around the spending.
We can look at the American example. President Ronald Reagan cut deeply into social programs and expanded the military budget. He ballooned the military budget. I must say it is sad that the Canadian Government is starting to reflect that same set of priorities in which it, with its most recent Budget and expenditure announcements, is expanding the military budget at the same time as it continues to hold social programs under threat. When it comes to spending and deficits, it is not a question of spending or not spending, it is a question of where the spending is and what are the priorities.
Therefore I ask the question, what has the Government done to address the critical and key issues that face our generation, the questions of poverty, homelessness, and functional illiteracy? What is happening with regard to employment for all? There are one million people in this country looking for work who can find no work. There is still a differential between what men are paid and what women are paid. Native people in this country suffer from extremely high levels of unemployment. On Indian reserves there is something like 80 per cent unemployment. If that existed for white, European ancestry Canadians we would have a revolution in this country. Why do we tolerate those types of injustice? Why has the Government taken no significant action in those areas?
What about visible minorities in terms of employment? There are ethnic people who come here with talents, abilities, skills and qualifications who are not recognized and who must be recognized. There are people from other countries who are trained as doctors, nurses, architects, and engineers whose qualifications are recognized in the United States but are not recognized here. What about a little justice. What about a little action. If it takes a little expenditure, why do we not do it in this area instead of forgiving the taxes of those 60,000 Canadian corporations that have profits of hundreds of millions of dollars and pay no tax. When it comes to deficits, when it comes to borrowing, it is a question of where is the Government spending the money and what are its priorities.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 am pleased to participate in the debate on the request by the federal Government for authority from the House of Commons to borrow $25 billion. It gives me an opportunity to address

March 1, 1988
Borrowing Authority
and focus on the Government's fiscal arrangements and plans following on the heels of the most recent Budget.
Many things have been said about the Budget by many commentators. I have the honour of representing the riding of York West in this Chamber. In my opinion, the recent Budget is mostly about taxes and missed opportunities; taxes, which come after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) very clearly stated during and immediately after the last federal election that they would not impose tax increases on Canadian citizens; missed opportunities, because yet again it was another window of opportunity to redress some of the unfair measures experienced by Canadians. A Budget should be an attempt to redress, balance, and ensure that there is equity and fairness in the system for all Canadians regardless of who they are, what they make, or where they live.
It would be incorrect to focus on one Budget at the exclusion of the other Budgets that have been presented by the Government. Those Budgets should be taken together and addressed as a collective package that signals a direction in which the Government wants to take the country. However, this is primarily a Budget about increased taxes which runs contrary to the commitments that the Government and its leader so clearly posed to the Canadian electorate.
In spite of what the Minister of Finance states, there are more tax increases in 1988 than indicated in the Budget. First, previous Budgets have considerably increased taxes. Second, the Government has built in tax increases. The tax system through tax brackets, family allowance, and child tax credits has been partially de-indexed, so those are hidden increases. Third, tax reform has also introduced new tax increases for 1988. There has been a 10 per cent tax on long distance calls for a value of close to $900 million. There has been a 12 per cent tax on wallpaper, paint, and related products for a value of close to $60 million. There has also been the excise tax on gasoline.
Since the Conservative Party took office in September, 1984 the excise tax on gasoline has been increased by 5 cents a litre or 23 cents a gallon. Think of that, 23 cents a gallon, Madam Speaker. Some time back Canadians made a very clear determination about a previous Tory administration that wanted to increase that tax by 18 cents. That 23 cents a gallon is made up of the following increases. In September, 1985 there was an increase of 2 cents a litre; a further 1 cent increase in January, 1987; another 1 cent increase in February, 1987; and with the latest Budget there will be another 1 cent per litre increase in April of this year.
Another statistic of which we must be cognizant is that since the Conservative Party came to power in 1984 the tax paid by individuals has increased by 68 per cent. If one translates that into a dollar value it is $29.3 billion. In comparison, taxes paid by corporations only increased by 28 per cent or $2.6 billion. On top of that, if that is not enough of an imbalance, there are 60,000 profitable corporations in our communities that do not
pay taxes, even after the much heralded tax reform package of the Government.
The impact of the inequities of this tax distribution will be painfully experienced by average families across the nation. For a family of four, comprising two adults and two children, whose income is $32,000, the tax increases brought about by the cumulative effect of previous Budgets aggravated by this Budget will amount to $1,200 per family, even after the tax reform announcements by the Minister of Finance.
What does that mean in real terms for the average family? I did an analysis up to the 1987 Budget which was aggravated by the numbers presented by the Minister a few short weeks ago. After the 1987 Budget the cumulative effect on a family earning $15,000 was to increase the share of their taxes by close to 70 per cent compared to 1984. In an income bracket of $30,000 there was an increase of 17 per cent. For a $50,000 wage earner there was an increase of 9.5 per cent. A person who earned over $100,000 had an increase of 3.8 per cent. On the one hand there is a staggering 70 per cent increase on a family least able to afford any increases, and on the other side of the equation there is not even a 4 per cent increase for a $100,000 wage earner.
When one looks at the tax system, the tax increases, and the disproportionate amounts that Canadians have to pay on their salaries, those increases have to be described as inequitable and unfair. As our Leader pointed out in his address on the Budget, one could discuss the entire Budget and the Government by talking about two different types of Canada and two different types of Canadians. We have fiscal measures which impose disproportionate increases on those individuals earning from $15,000 to $20,000 per year. When we see families earning hundreds of thousands of dollars a year paying very little increase and corporations not paying a cent, we must begin to ask ourselves what type of country we are trying to build.
People are coming to me in my constituency with the everyday problem of trying to make ends meet at the end of the month. Working husbands and wives with families who are trying to carry their mortgages, educate, feed, and clothe their children are all too often faced with a desperate situation at the end of the month. They are beginning to say that those people who consider themselves to be part of the middle class segment of Canadian society are Finding it more difficult to stay within that middle class.
It seems that the growing disparity, which is aggravated by Budgets, is beginning to erode the middle class segment of society. We have individuals who once considered themselves to be in the middle class of society falling either on the side of the "haves" or unfortunately and regrettably on the side of the "have-nots". That is the gulf of disparity between the two Canadas upon which the Government and Parliament should focus. That is the gulf of disparity which is the result of


March 1, 1988

statistics that can be quoted to prove any point. We must try to bridge that growing disparity rather than fuel or increase it.
If we look at a number of socio-economic problems in society, we can draw a link to the impact of fiscal measures and Budgets on Canadians. Here we are in 1988 in a very prosperous, fortunate, and progressive country like Canada. However, have we ever asked ourselves, when we visit Vancouver, Toronto, or Montreal, which are among the more prosperous centres in our country, why the line-ups at the food banks and soup kitchens are getting longer? Why is it that churches in some of those cities are collecting and distributing food on Saturdays and Sundays for those who cannot provide for themselves? Line-ups such as these were not even seen at the height of the depression many years ago or even when we were in the crisis of war. However, these line-ups not only exist in 1988 but they are getting longer.
Food banks in Metropolitan Toronto are getting busier. For example, the North York Harvest Food Bank in my riding is continuing to mobilize its citizens to collect food for those who cannot provide for themselves. Many people in my working class-middle class riding of York West cannot believe that the problem exists. Perhaps it is more of a hidden problem and this is why the food bank has trouble trying to mobilize Canadians to help their fellow man.
We have tried to help the North York Harvest Food Bank by having Christmas food drives, not only to increase the intake of food but to educate and mobilize the Canadian community to rally for its fellow citizens.
In terms of more collective or global imagery, what does it say for this country when we have growing line-ups? It says that something, somewhere in the system, must be incorrect. If those men, women, and children who line up for soup, sandwiches, and other groceries had an option, they would not do so. There might be some abuse here or there in terms of people who come to expect it or come to rely on these line-ups. However, the vast majority of individuals would not be there if they were able to fend and provide for themselves. I cannot think of anything more humbling or more shameful to the individual sense of pride than telling society, by the fact that they are in a line-up, that somehow they have failed to put food on the table for their families. That is a profound statement. It attacks the very sense of identity or sense of purpose of Canadian citizens.
Thank God for the churches and the non-profit organizations which have picked up the slack in trying to meet that real need. These line-ups should be a signal to the elected leadership of the country in this Parliament that something is wrong and that it must be addressed. Through fiscal management, through our Budgets, and through planning how money is spent, we can alter the status of the undignified identity of lining up in the mornings and evenings. We cannot allow it to go unnoticed.
Borrowing Authority
Why is it that there are more homeless people in society today? Why is it that major centres with the greatest prosperity have the largest number of people who are homeless or do not have shelter? Once again, thank God for non-profit organizations, churches, and the various other elements in our community which have mobilized to try to come to grips with that situation. Is it not a by-product of something which is wrong in this system? Why is it that poverty is on the increase? Why is it that an increased number of single, female-led families now find themselves below the poverty line? The mother or both parents are to fend for themselves, but we do not have adequate day care facilities and their children are unattended. Does that not then become a societal problem rather than an individual, family-related difficulty which they must overcome?
What about the number of job increases which the Government likes to read out in the House of Commons every second Friday afternoon when it gets the statistics? What about the fact that the majority of those job increases are part-time jobs, low-paying jobs, or jobs which do not offer security from one Friday to the next, despite the bravado imagery of the Government saying that it has somehow succeeded in creating the types of jobs Canadians want?
What about the different regions of our country, not the Torontos, the Montreals, or the Vancouvers? What happens to the Monctons, to the Sault Ste. Maries, and to the Sudburys of the country? What happens to single industry towns that do not enjoy the same benefits as fellow citizens in other centres? Can we not begin to redress those imbalances as well?
Of course we can, if there is the political will, the political courage, and the political dignity to say that it is not a question of how much we spend or where we spend it, but a question of how we spend it, how we create Budgets, and for whom the fiscal measures are intended. Are they to widen the gap? Are they to increase the line-ups? Are they to keep the Monctons of the country Monctons rather than to have them become centres of prosperity? Are they intended to increase the number of single, female-led families now below the poverty line?
If we have the collective courage to try to redress the experiences faced by such Canadians, why do we not do it? Why is it that a family which earns $15,000 a year has an increase in its taxes by closes to 70 per cent while a family earning $100,000 has to face an increase of only 2 per cent?
All Canadians are realistic about taxes. They know that taxes are here to stay. They do not mind using the tax system to provide the goods and values that we have as a social contract in Canada. We do not mind paying our way to provide a health system, a school system, a system of civilization that many other countries do not have. I think of those countries we visit during our vacation times which have beautiful resort areas, that provide us with satisfaction for a

March 1, 1988
Borrowing Authority
week or two, countries where, if we go beyond the periphery of the resort area, we see how other people in this world live. When we return to Canada we give a degree of thanks for the system that we enjoy. We also realize that we have to pay for our system. I believe that the average Canadian in my riding, and in yours, Madam Speaker, is realistic about the system and the costs of maintaining our lifestyle.
Canadians are becoming frustrated and angry when they perceive, and know, that different Canadians are being asked to pay a different amount for the system. That is where disparity starts and cynicism is bred. That is where Canadians become less enchanted about Canada and the lot in which they find themselves. If people felt that the burden was shared, being carried by those who are rich, wealthy and who have worked hard to reach that position, then the inequity would be removed.
For the first time, according to our polling studies, people are beginning to classify themselves in class structures. I close by saying that is, indeed, a very dangerous signal to our elected leadership. Lord knows, we have had our differences and fights between east and west. We have had them between the anglophones, the francophones and the multicultural communities. We have tried to bridge those differences. Never have we in Canada had the struggle which other countries have had, like Great Britain, over class stratification. Yet for the first time in Canadian history, according to our polls, the reaction of Canadians is beginning to indicate that there is a greater class stratification taking place, a stratification between those who are in the have and have-not categories. This is the stratification of two types of Canada. I hope that the Government comes to realize that that gulf of disparity between those two Canadas is widening, and that it is time for the bridge to be built once again.

Madam Speaker, I have been listening with interest to the speech by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi). I have the pleasure of serving with him on the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism working together in that vital aspect of national life.
I was interested in the earlier part of his speech in which he spoke about the lack of fairness in the Canadian tax system. He stated some of the most important statistics, such as the reality of 60,000 profitable corporations which are not being taxed at all, along with the failure of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to tap profits which might be used very easily to reduce the deficit and the borrowing which is such a burden on Canadians.
1 was interested to hear the Hon. Member from York West, who is a Liberal Member, talk about these things. He spoke about the growing disparity and the development of wealth for some few and the experience of poverty for others, but that predates 1984. The situation has certainly been getting worse and worse to such an extent that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recognized last year that we were developing two Canadas. He expressed alarm, although when you see what his
Government has been doing you would think it was fostering a prosperous Canada, letting an undeveloped poor Canada develop and that that is the way it will be. But that predates 1984.
The tax system we are talking about, which admittedly has been made so much worse, is one that developed from the 1970s, from the time the first Trudeau Government buckled under enormous corporate pressure and abandoned the principles of the Carter Royal Commission on taxation. We had the Benson budgets in those days and changes to taxation which the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) as Finance Minister a dozen years ago and more was perpetrating at the time. These are the people who built the system.
I find it a bit contradictory that my good friend should be making this fine speech, when his leader is as responsible as anyone for the early development of this system which had really unfortunate social consequences by the late 1980s. I invite the Hon. Member's reaction to the observations on political contradictions which the Liberal Party is having to experience.

1 thank the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay- Nipigon (Mr. Epp) for his observations. There is a vertical mosaic in this country, quoting Julian Porter's book, but to a certain degree I think the Hon. Member from Thunder Bay is misrepresenting what I have tried to convey to this Chamber. I am not here to make a defence, to apologize for any previous administration. I challenge the Member to go back to the days when Canada was led by a Liberal Government. We had a poll the other day which compared the Government of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with the Government of Mr. Trudeau. The numbers painted a very interesting picture of how Canadians judged a Liberal administration compared to a Tory administration. If there are people, particularly among the New Democratic Party, who suggest that there is no difference between a Tory and a Liberal, let the numbers speak for themselves and let this philosophy of their vision of Canada as defined through budgets lay to rest those questions fueled by individuals who want to blur the picture.
Canadians came to realize, particularly after the expectations generated by this Government, the very simple and clear difference between an administration led by a Liberal Party and an administration led by a Conservative Party. Under those Liberal administrations, I challenge the Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon to show me one instance when the regions were cut adrift as they are today. Show me an era when the food bank lineups were longer than they are today. Show me an era when the disparity of income tax distribution
March 1, 1988

was such that a person earning $200,000 had an increase of 2 per cent while an individual earning $15,000 had to submit to a 60 to 70 per cent increase. I challenge the Elon. Member to provide me with those details.
1 am not suggesting that all the ills were cured by previous administrations. We have continued Government in order to try to better the lives of individuals and to try to make society a little more progressive than it was when we found it. In those previous administrations though, there was an attempt to bridge the gulf that existed then and that is being aggravated today.
I ended my earlier remarks by dealing with the question of polling. That too is a very interesting phenomenon. When Canadians were polled about their views under previous Liberal administrations, never did it surface that there was a perception of class stratification, the perception that Canadians were being compartmentalized according to what they earned and the lifestyles they were able to enjoy. For the first time in a long time, Canadians are beginning to perceive themselves and society in terms of class stratification. We should avoid that and take the lesson of the difficulties in Great Britain.
Great Britain too is a world power and certainly a strength to be reckoned with. In Great Britain, there are very monumental problems with the perception of class stratification. We in Canada have always avoided those struggles that pit one Canadian against another, based on class.
I suggest to the Hon. Member, whose Party has not had any experience leading the country on a national level, and probably will not have that experience for a long time to come, that he also deal with the facts and ask Canadians to measure the administrations they have experienced. The Hon. Member will find the same result that this recent poll illustrated, which is that previous Liberal administrations were respected for their leadership, their integrity and their vision of things to come. They were not perceived as Governments that were bankrupt based on commitments, and bankrupt in a clear direction with which to take a progressive Canada, taking only one type of Canada forward and leaving the other behind.

Madam Speaker, I would have hesitated to rise, knowing that others might want to join the debate, but my friend-although it may be a trying friendship-has challenged me to say something about specific matters. Let me point to one general and one specific matter regarding the failings of the previous Liberal Government.
I remember very well the disappointment felt by local Governments when the Trudeau Government decided to cancel the Winter Works projects which had begun first under the Diefenbaker Government back in the 1960s. Those programs allowed local Governments to obtain federal government assistance to carry out construction projects in the wintertime. The cancellation of those programs was one of the ways regions were slighted in their development possibilities.
Borrowing Authority
More specifically, I think of Thunder Bay, which is not exactly a one-industry town, though still all too dependent on transportation and resource industries in northern Ontario. That community was put by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion in the same category as Metro Toronto when it came to obtaining assistance for local industrial development. It was regarded as being in the prosperous half of the country. We certainly felt cast adrift by the Liberal Government, even though we had strong representation, it would seem, from previous Members like Mr. Robert Andras who held cabinet positions in the 1970s.
I realize that I will not have the time to do my harangue on the shortcomings of successive Liberal Governments and the way in which Trudeau Governments disappointed the Canadian people. For example, the first Liberal Government of 1968 held the just society vision which so failed the Canadian public that the Liberals almost lost the 1972 election. Over the next two years it was more responsive to the Canadian people and won the 1974 election. 1 could go on with this record of political infamy, but I realize that I am transgressing the limits of time. Thank you, Madam Speaker, for allowing me to say that much.

It is one thing to ask Canadians to comment on a Government during the life of one administration because there are always the gives and takes, the passions of the immediate debates, that cloud the imagery. It would be very interesting to look into Canadians' perceptions of those Governments after they have come and gone.
When we go into the next election, that perception will be weighed very heavily and very carefully. Canadians will begin to compare what they have had for the last four years with the programs, policies, leadership and honesty they enjoyed before. subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-CRITICISM OF CANADA'S NEGOTIATING STANCE

Mr. Speaker, since April 1987, when the Unemployment Insurance Act deprived early retirees of their vested right to draw unemployment insurance benefits, protest groups started to form.

After contributing to the Unemployment Insurance Fund for many years, during which most of them never drew any benefits at all, they now stand to lose $15,000 in benefits because their pension fund is now considered to be a salary for the purposes of unemployment insurance.
Now that they have been deprived of their benefits, a number of early retirees are wondering about the billion-and-a-half-dollar surplus in the Unemployment Insurance Fund. subsubtopic: ETHNIC CULTURAL ACTIVITIES-PROVISION OF FINANCIAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the failure of the federal cultural agencies to support ethnic cultural activity is a longstanding grievance in Canada's ethnocultural communities. This failure is the failure of the Canada Council, for example, to act on the multicultural policy statement of 1971.
In spite of the Prime Minister's declaration in 1971 that Canada had no official culture and that the Government of Canada would foster the various cultures, the Department of Communications remained preoccupied with the cultures of English-speaking and French-speaking Canada. Cultural activities in the other ethnocultural communities were left to the Multiculturalism Directorate of the Department of Secretary of State.
This practice of leaving the ethnocultural communities in ghettos of neglect must end. A Canadian Government committed to multiculturalism must ensure that the Canada Council and other agencies respect the policies of multiculturalism. These agencies need to be provided with the financial resources to foster a diversity of cultures.
Only by such action will we overcome the divisions of the past and realize the richness that ethnocultural diversity brings to Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADA SEVER TIES WITH SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. 1 want to point out how frequently the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have said that Canada would break diplomatic relations with South Africa and would impose total economic sanctions against South Africa unless there was meaningful progress in the dismantling of apartheid.
The Prime Minister and his Minister committed Canada to a full severing of relations with South Africa on September 13, 1985; October 23, 1985; June 6, 1986; September 9, 1987, and yesterday, February 29, 1988. Indeed, for two and one-half years Canadians have been told by the Government that there would be a total severing of relationships with South Africa and for two and one-half years the situation, instead of getting better, has gotten worse.
When is the Government going to carry out its commitments made by the Prime Minister of this country, both in the United Nations and in Parliament, to sever ties with South Africa now that no progress has been made in the dismantling of apartheid?
