In designing this legislation, I would be remiss if I did not pay tribute to my Cabinet colleagues, particularly those from western Canada, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), and individuals from the western region of Canada, who put forward their views and concerns and who assisted in designing this program.

March 1, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
The Government sees Canada as a land of mutually supporting regions in which the prosperity flows from the broad economic base throughout the country.
From downtown Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I am sure that the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. Benjamin) will take part in this debate, and 1 know that he will support the legislation designed to bring benefit to his constituents as well as mine.
There have been several organizational experiments over the past 60 years to promote regional and economic development in Canada. I would suggest that there has been little measurable progress.
One thing that has been clear from those experiments is that Ottawa-based centralized approaches fail to capture the regional differences that we all recognize in Canada. They failed to provide federal policies which are tailored to the individual needs of the men and women in each region of Canada. The West's development problems are not the same as those of Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario, or Quebec.
When this Government came to office we came with ideas of how to make regional development work. We made a commitment to ensure that the regions of Canada would have a strong voice in influencing economic development.
The first half of this mandate was designed to create the right environment, the economic growth, and the investment that was needed. It was also designed to correct some sectorial inadequacies that were apparent, such as those in energy, agriculture, taxation, trade, and in other sectors. The groundwork has been done and the base has been established. Regional development can only take place when the climate for national economic development is right.
Once the climate was created, new tools for regional economic development were put in place. In June the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced the creation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency; in July the Northern Ontario Development Fund was announced; and on August 4, 1987 the Prime Minister announced the new western diversification initiative. These are regional initiatives, and they are major undertakings to correct regional imbalances and inadequacies.
In the past under DREE, DRIE, and all the others, of which there have been several, regional economic development policy and regional economic program delivery were never successfully married.
The legislation before the House at this time brings the policy development and the program delivery together. The policy role, which would be combined with the instruments of the Western Economic Development Fund, will allow us to have the tools to do the job.
A major component of the initiative is the department with headquarters in Edmonton and offices in Winnipeg, Saskatoon, and Vancouver. It is to promote diversification from regional ideas. It is not an Ottawa-imposed approach to the economic development of the West. It is close to the people whom it is designed to serve. It is not located in Ottawa, but in the West. It will also bring a western voice to the formation of national policy. All Ministers, regardless of their ministry responsibilities, always speak on behalf of their regions and will continue to do that. What we are doing now is putting in statute and legislating a department which will speak and attempt to influence national policies in order that those national policies can better serve people in western Canada.
When we look at the areas that are important, to mention some, agriculture, forestry, transport, science and technology, it is important to draw those agencies and departments together and to examine the programs and the policies in relation to the economic development potential in western Canada.
I believe there is an opportunity to influence Government without expenditures. As an example, in the August Budget we were able to work as a pathfinder where kaolin was classified as a mineral. That is the first change in the schedule since potash was recognized as a mineral some 20 years ago. It seems strange to me, since it was not a vegetable and it was mined out of the ground, that it was not classified as a mineral. It had to be classified as a mineral in order that the tax regime available to mining could be put in place. That was recognized by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and announced in the Budget of February 10.
I do not think it is misstating a fact, and my colleague from Saskatchewan will recognize it, but it is almost twice as far from Ottawa to Regina than it is from Regina to Ottawa. That is a fact of life that we have recognized for a long period of time.
The department will work as a pathfinder for those men and women in western Canada who have ideas and proposals, who want to do business with the Government of Canada, and who want to assist us in strengthening the economy in the West. It will serve as a voice in western Canada to promote cooperative ventures with the provinces, business, labour, and other public and private organizations. The department will also have the following responsibilities. It will formulate plans and integrate federal strategies to support the economic diversification of the western economy. It will oversee or implement such plans and strategies, if they are not implemented by other Ministries. It will promote the growth of small and medium-sized businesses. It will attempt to improve the business environment in western Canada. It will support economic and policy research. Finally, it will engage in and conclude co-operative arrangements with the provinces.
March 1, 1988

Fundamentally this legislation outlines how the federal Government can better serve western Canadians. It is a different approach from that of any other Government. It integrates in legislation a regional voice in government processes, policy-making, and program delivery.
Another key element of the legislation is the financial assistance which can be made available through the department for the development and diversification of the western economy. This means that the federal Government can become actively involved in the implementation of key diversification projects and programs.
The department will offer assistance to enterprises which have prospects of furthering the diversification or strengthening and expanding the economy of the West.
This assistance will be incremental. It will be "top up" or "last in" support for key business and economic projects in the West. The "topping up" or "last in" support is not to take away from assistance provided by other government Departments. We must also consider the client's own contribution to a project. Equity is important, whether it comes in the form of individual funding or from financial institutions. These projects will not be all government support; some initiative and some equity must be put forward. If we can take advantage of strategic development opportunities in the West, proposals that have the greatest potential for broadening and expanding the economic base of the West, we will do so.
This is not an entitlement program. If we take a look at previous experiences, entitlement was part of it. This program is not entitlement; it is managed with flexibility and creativity. We will see what projects must be and should be supported.
To enhance the flexibility we have a number of principles, not guidelines or automatic kick-outs. We believe that as time goes on we will gain experience and more knowledge about the way to handle the co-ordinating and funding functions of the department.
Basically one principle is aimed at business and economic projects which can expand or diversify the economy in western Canada, projects which lead to new products, new markets, new technologies, import substitution, and new long-term jobs. As 1 mentioned, it will be used to top up the last dollar in. Therefore, there must be a comprehensive search of other government programs and other government Departments which could and should assist in a major way to strengthen the economy in the West.
There will be a range of types and levels of assistance. For example, there will be loan guarantees, credit and loan insurance, contributions, repayable contributions, and grants. All economic sectors will be eligible, including the service sector which is the fastest growing sector in the Canadian economy, particularly in western Canada. It will also include the natural resource sector, which is very important in western Canada, wherein clearly there is an opportunity to develop new
Western Economic Diversification Act
products and new lines. Projects such as research and development and marketing will be encouraged, projects which help build a business support structure. These projects will enhance the competitive capacity, so that a large number of western Canadians can take advantage of the business support structure which will be put in place. There will also be support for individual business proposals, after they have been accepted, assessed, and viewed in terms of their ability to expand the economy in western Canada.
There has been criticism of tardiness and over-long reviews in projects. Because we are working on a principle rather than a guideline, and because we do not have a slide-rule or an automatic percentage, it takes a little longer to review or assess each proposal. Because of the flexibility that has been built into it, there had to be some reorganization of Government. I think that was necessary and desirable in the establishment of the new department. The federal economic development coordinators and their offices in the western provinces were transferred from the Department of Regional and Industrial Expansion to form the core of the new department.
The approach for which we are looking is to develop strategic partnerships to avoid duplication. We hope to be able to optimize the process of expansion of the economy in western Canada. If something needs an extra push or more drive, if it is something we want to force- feed, there will be dollars available to top up that initiative.
We have recognized-and it was recognized by the Prime Minister western Canada needed an advocate in central Government. This legislation establishes a department of western diversification. It is already having an impact. The challenges and policies which are designed as national policies will have to take into account the country's regional dimension.
I will be interested in some of the comments of members of the federal Liberal Opposition with respect to the attention they paid to the West during all their years in office.
Stick around and you will hear about them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I will stick around. I remember a $4 billion fund which vanished, totally disappeared.
The department takes over a number of existing programs in other areas and will serve as a pathfinder for business. It will assist business in doing government work and in having access to Government. What we need is the strategic capability to seize the opportunities put forward by western Canadians. We will be able to give action and life to the visions of Canadian men and women. Basically, the new department will have the interests of small business and medium sized business as its main responsibility.
We cannot achieve this objective alone, but I believe that we have the tools to achieve it. We will have the ability to fund it, and we will have the assistance of the other Ministries. Certainly there are people in western Canada with the desire and the tenacity to make it work.

March 1, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
Regionally based approaches are different. This is something that is not understood by people in other Parties. It establishes relationships within line Departments. It also establishes relationships with the central agencies in the federal Government. It will have the co-ordinating role of a central agency and, in the management of the fund, it will have the operational role of a line Department. If we are to influence the national policies of the Government, we must ensure that it is properly linked with other federal Departments.
There will be an informal group of Ministers to deal with western economic concerns and a more formal Deputy Ministers' meeting, chaired by the Deputy Minister of Western Economic Diversification.
There has been a great deal of interest in the program in western Canada. Western Canadians are eager to participate. By mid-February we had received over 40,000 inquiries, had held some 3,000 meetings with individuals, and received in some form 2,355 proposals. We have processed some 262 proposals.
Some of the systems that have been made available to business in general, which will benefit not just individuals but have a systemic approach, is our participation in a $25.5 million program by contributing $5 million to the potash institute of Canada to diversify market opportunities in Asia and to strengthen leading-edge research and education facilities of the Saskatoon-based institutions. As a form of partnership, the provincial Government in this project has provided $6.8 million and the industry $13.8 million, for a total of over $25.5 million.
Toward the establishment of an $18 million world class cold climate engineering research facility in Edmonton, the centre for frontier engineering research, $7.5 million was contributed. That, again, was a partnership between the provincial Government of Alberta, with its contribution of $6.8 million and the balance being contributed by industry.
In British Columbia, $9.45 million of a $21 million project went toward the establishment of a marketing program for the B.C. shake and shingle industry. The industry is contributing $11.5 million in that joint initiative.
There have been other projects, some smaller and some larger. An example of a small initiative in Moose Jaw is the Huff and Puff Stitchery. It is receiving a grant to expand the capacity of its business. The western diversification office is assisting a company to design and manufacture motor control panels for the use in electrical installations. Another company will be using western diversification money to manufacture donkey heads or pump jacks used in the oil fields of the West.
There will be more, Madam Speaker. Again, I want to emphasize that in reviewing each proposal and treating each proposal as in individual initiative it does require a little more
effort and time, but I believe it is very beneficial to those interested in expanding the economy of western Canada. We will not have tier systems. The West will be treated as one region. The tier system was not beneficial to western Canada in the past and it will not be beneficial at this time.
In the past seven months we have been working and designing a new department and a new approach to regional development. We have designed and determined how to administer $1.2 billion. We have responded to the overwhelming public interest in this initiative. We have made substantial and effective investments in western Canada. As always, in creating a new department, one has a challenge. I must say that although the agenda is full, I am confident that with the energy, the enthusiasm and the real knowledge of individual western Canadian men and women the new department, over the coming years, will have made an appreciable and permanent impact upon the economic diversification and strength of western Canada.
It is a program designed by western Canadians. It is a program that is headquartered in western Canada, and it is a program that will bring benefit to all of Canada by strengthening one region of Canada.

Madam Speaker, in opening this debate on the proposed legislation for western diversification, I think it is important for us to draw to the attention of the House a story that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of yesterday which quotes the Chairman of the Manitoba Conservative caucus saying that "it will very helpful if the provincial Government did not criticize. It may end up getting more assistance in the western diversification". The story goes on that it is a basically "go along or get nothing" program. That is the import of the story.
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

-or it will not get any grants, if they do not have to fit the particular political equation or standards.
There has been, I think, over the years, a basic standard of regional development, namely, that all regions and provinces get treated fairly and equitably, and one does not simply use things as political clubs to try to enforce compliance of specific measures if it is the considered opinion of a provincial Government that something is in the best interests or not in the best interests of its citizens. But this is not the way the so-called western diversification fund is being used. It is clearly politicizing in a highly sort of partisan way the use of federal funds in economic development, but not economic development that has any plan, rhyme, reason or blueprint to it; it is simply used as a basis of slushing those who you are in agreement with either in a partisan way-
That is the way the Liberals did things.

-or where you are trying to enforce a kind of provincial government agreement to go along or give up.
The Minister in introducing his program said it was innovative, different and expansive and that it would do all these new things. I do not know where the Minister has been. This program for western diversification has far less money than was committed under previous Liberal Governments. It has a far less organizational base to it and it will be far less effective. Let me recite a few facts to the Minister while he sits there and giggles like a little boy who is caught with his finger in the plug.

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Here comes the invisible fund now.

Yes, let us talk about the invisible fund, the $4 billion committed under the Western Development Fund under the previous Government. Of the fund, $3.5 billion went into railway modernization. That was based upon extensive consultation with all the farms groups, all provincial Governments, and it was based on what is the single most important investment that could be made in western Canada, namely, to modernize the transportation system substantially. The Minister from Saskatchewan should know that if you do not
Western Economic Diversification Act
have an effective, efficient transportation system, you do not move potash, grain or logs.
In the late 1970s the railways were refusing to invest capital in the transportation system of the West. It was absolutely necessary for the federal Government to take the initiative to ensure a major investment in the infrastructure of western Canada. That was the $3.5 billion fund. That was not invisible money. That was cash and it is still being paid out.
The other part of the money, a $250 million fund, went for native economic development, which the Minister responsible should know something about. This Minister has deliberately frustrated that fund and has not given it the kind of encouragement or incentive to develop enterprises, businesses and activities for native people in western Canada. The economic plight of the native people was also identified as the single most important social and economic problem facing western Canada. We set up a bank to provide funding so they could start their own businesses and projects to help the aboriginal peoples throughout the West and in the Territories. This Government, not happy to see that kind of self initiative undertaken by native people, basically closed down that fund and basically, again, turned it into a slush fund. The Minister giggles and laughs, but I have told you, Madam Speaker, where the money went on that program.
In 1983-84, $1.2 billion was committed to western Canada in a two-year period under the ERDA agreements. In fact, that generated a total of $2.1 billion because we got matching funds from the provinces. The Minister says that nothing has ever been done before, but the fact is that the commitment of a specific regional fund for western Canada was twice what this Government is committing in terms of economic development funds.
It is true that in 1984 when this Government came to power, it cut back on many of those programs. It cancelled many of those programs. It stood in the way of many of those programs. The fact is that those commitments were made.
Once again, these agreements were signed in full cooperation and consultation with the provinces and each province was able to establish its priorities. They were able to work out with the municipalities clear objectives for each of the provinces. The agreements were signed, sealed legal documents, part of the regional fund. What happened, of course, is that Tories do not like successes, particularly those of other Governments, and so if they did not like the nature of the previous Government, they stood in the way.
At the same time, we had also committed substantial additional funds for employment and training. The Economic Council report had said that one of the most important areas for investment in the West was to upgrade substantially its workforce. Last year, Employment and Immigration spent $479 million in western Canada. For the next forecast year, according to the Estimates, $339 million will be spent, a net

reduction of $140 million. Is this the kind of influence the Minister is saying the western diversification agency will have? That in fact is down several hundreds of millions of dollars from where it was in 1984.
This is the great example of how the new agency will show western Canadians what kind of muscle it has around the cabinet table. The West will lose $140 million unemployment and training funds for western Canada. I would say that the Minister should be embarrassed and ashamed to claim that kind of influence when in fact all that happens is that projects are lost.
We talked about the need to expand scientific research and development. Under the previous mandate, we put the hydrology lab in Saskatoon, we established a cold water lab in Edmonton, we established-

Let us talk about the organizational question, which is very important. The Minister spoke about the need to show organized and co-ordinated activities at the federal level. What happened to the western cabinet committee that provided a co-

ordination unit at the highest level? It was not comprised of civil servants or Deputy Ministers. The western cabinet committee ensured-

speechtext: How many Members from western Canada were on it, elected Members, Lloyd? Elected?

The proof of the effectiveness of that committee was in what was delivered. The Tories disbanded that cabinet committee. They got rid of its political influence. They neglected that opportunity to continue having a special committee of Cabinet for western Canada that would ensure at the highest levels of decision-making, reporting directly to the Planning and Priorities Committee, co-ordination and influence and the assurance that other activities of the Government would be properly construed.
The difference is that when we were in power, the CN was not laying off people in Winnipeg and Edmonton. The railways were not closing down. Canada Packers plants were not closing down. Projects were not being cancelled because we were able to make our case at the cabinet table. In fact, this Government is relying upon a group of civil servants to cover for it. That is what it is trying to pretend is great co-ordination.
Further to that, we had established in each of the provinces a federal economic development co-ordinator responsible for organizing and co-ordinating all the activities of all the federal agencies at that level and developing and instituting plans that would be made at the local and regional levels in full consultation with the provinces, the municipalities and the local business sector. That program was very effective and useful in ensuring that there were bottom-up developmental plans. An example of this would be the core area initiative in the City of Winnipeg and the North Portage development program. With an investment of $90 million in federal, provincial and municipal money, organized primarily by federal initiative, we were able to generate over $400 million in private capital.
This Government talks about the need to generate new activity in the private sector. However, it tends to forget that there must be a serious, clear blueprint developed in each of the regions, not simply a political slush fund. By the way, and I bring this to the attention of the House, it is unfortunate that specifically excluded in western diversification is the opportunity for urban redevelopment or community development programs. Specifically excluded is any investment in social programs that would provide incentives for people at the lower level to participate in western growth.
We have the example of the core area initiative started in 1980-81. It was a combination of physical redevelopment downtown, encouragement of small business, and the use of federal facilities such as the Air Canada buildings and the NRC centres. There was funding of special community-based social programs to help native people get training to move into the workforce, help senior citizens develop their own housing projects, and help residents of that area to develop some sense
Western Economic Diversification Act
of initiative for self-development. We did not exclude certain groups from assistance. It was a recognition that parts of the core areas of cities in western Canada such as Winnipeg, Regina and Calgary, as well as the small communities, were suffering a terrible erosion.
One of the most important tools for economic development is the upgrading and refurbishing of the basic infrastructure of communities. You are not going to attract new business if you have a deteriorating core area. You are not going to get a new factory placed in a small community in Manitoba or Saskatchewan if you no longer have decent sewer lines, proper transportation, or if your school system is failing. You are not going to be able to attract new R and D centres if the universities in those areas are beginning to erode. Yet those areas are excluded under this plan. That flies in the face of some of the best and most useful practical examples, some of which we pioneered in the West.
The initiative we took in the core areas, while not perfect, was a demonstration of how you can combine social investment and economic development investment in a package to provide not only the refurbishing of a city but also to give people a chance.
About 40 per cent of new workers in western Canada will be native people. Unfortunately they come in without proper education or training. If they do not receive the kind of support necessary to become fully participating members of the workforce, then the economic development of western Canada will not occur. You cannot have 40 per cent of your workforce idle. You cannot have that kind of terrible tragedy taking place in front of you. Yet where is there in the plan any kind of program that addresses that fundamental issue in western Canada? Or that comes to grips with one of the most serious social and economic problems in Canada, certainly in western Canada? There is nothing here to provide the slightest bit of assistance or support to meet that very serious issue. Yet if we do not meet it, it will cost western Canada through a waste of human talent and increasing costs to our social service system.
The only proven way to provide an antidote is through development incentives. As I pointed out in my speech yesterday, why is it that even the simple provision of job training grants is being denied these kinds of organizations? Young natives in the core area of Winnipeg are no longer being given the opportunity even to get in an employment program because "it does not fit the high-tech training philosophy of the Canadian Jobs Strategy". You are not going to develop western Canada unless you deal with that problem. It seems to me that any Government sitting down and trying to analyse a blueprint of what is necessary in the West would have put that foremost. Yet we have a statement here from the western diversification office that it is premature to indicate resource allocation by organizational structure.
I am particularly surprised at the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight). He of anyone in that Cabinet should be most cognizant of and sensitive to that

March 1, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
issue. When the opportunity came to put this issue forward as a clear priority, he ignored it totally. Ele has completely forgotten it. I simply say that this is not the way we will diversify the western economy.
Let me also point out another major economic exclusion which deals with the question of the need to develop major regional infrastructure programs. If you spend time talking to mayors and reeves of the smaller towns and bigger cities of western Canada, to provincial Ministers and many people in business, they realize that much of the infrastructure of western Canada has eroded. Look at the transportation and highway systems. We all know how fundamental transportation is to western Canada. It is our life-blood. It has enormous consequences. If we do not move the goods, we cannot sell them. Yet those systems are eroding. Provincial Governments have been cutting back. With the exception of the $3.5 billion that went into railway modernization, there has been very little going on.
Our highway system is in serious difficulty. We will have to substantially upgrade the transportation system. I am thinking in particular of the Port of Churchill. When I was in government we attempted to give that port new life. We attempted to upgrade its facilities to the point where they would be capable of offering new transportation opportunities in northern Canada. Four years later many of the projects under that agreement have still not been completed. The dust control system remains undone. That means the port is still languishing and uncertain about its future. Yet it is an alternative sea water port for the entire West. Here we are in this House talking about Arctic security, yet we are neglecting one of the most important ingredients, the transportation system. We are simply not talking about it.
The Minister talked about $42 million for a soil erosion program in Saskatchewan. I agree with it, but soil erosion is not going to be handled with $42 million. Look at the report done by Senator Sparrow and the Senate committee and you will see we are talking about hundreds of millions of dollars to arrest the erosion of western Canada's most valuable resource, its soil. We need a major water bank development project from British Columbia right through to Manitoba.
What an opportunity under this program to tackle that kind of program! We can say we will not look at specific little projects here and there but we will look at the need to establish a regional plan, something that will give focus to the entire region. If you look at the Saskatchewan River basin, the Columbia River basin, and the Fraser River basin, moving over the Rockies, you will recognize that all of the West is linked by its water system. It does not recognize provincial boundaries or federal constituencies. If we do not do something about that in the very near future, as the Senate report properly indicates, then the life-blood of western Canada is going to ooze away, as it is doing now. We are losing hundreds of thousands of hectares per year under present conditions. It is not a future problem, it is an immediate problem. It has to be done now.
That should be a priority. Development of native people should be a priority. Employment training must be a priority. The infrastructure of western Canada must be a priority. Those are the kinds of initiatives 1 would have expected the Government to be committed to doing something about.
I am particularly surprised because the Government said it does not want to tinker or provide a bunch of meaningless little grants and subsidies. It said that the way to encourage the private sector, agriculture, minerals and others, is to put a framework in place in which private dynamics can work. Yet somehow the Government seems to have reversed its stand and gone the other way. There is nothing whatsoever in this program, as I read it, that provides the slightest opportunity for westerners to come together as a region, or bring together the provinces, the federal Government, and major business, to ask what are the priorities for the region and then use federal investment in those areas.
Another example is in the study done by the Economic Council on western transition. It points out that in the future there should be entitlements for western Canada. The Minister denied that there will be any entitlements. The Economic Council basically said that there should be entitlements in certain key areas, one of which, of course, is education and research and development. We are moving into the information age and if we are to apply all kinds of new techniques and innovations to our agricultural and resource industries we must have a clear commitment to ensure that the work is done in western Canada.
They talk about centres of excellence in various places. I have no argument with that. As I pointed out, the Liberal Government had centres of excellence in hydrology, robotics, and other areas. However, why have a centre of excellence when the engineering faculties no longer have money even to do typing? The research grants of the federal Government are now driven by corporate donations. We do not have big corporations in western Canada to help in those areas and, as a result, we tend to be at the low end of the scale. If we are going to fund research programs by private sector contributions, if we are not going to provide the universities with the capacity to do basic research in those areas and give proper funding to the schools and colleges in western Canada, we will not have the people or facilities to keep abreast of the modern world of information and technology. That is the new entitlement which western Canada needs.
In the 1920s when our ancestors were fighting for entitlements they fought for the Crow rate. They said that the entitlement in Confederation was to ensure that we have a transportation system based upon a cost which we can afford. The new western entitlement must be in education and research and development. We must ensure that when the Government gives out big procurement contracts there is a fair
March I, 1988

sharing. There must be a requirement that when the Government provides support to the funding councils the regional requirement must be administered and met.
If I may digress for a moment, when we passed the Western Grain Transportation Act we wrote into the Bill a specific clause that said that the railroads must source in the region in which they are undertaking their major level of activity. We also put a $50 million Western Industrial Transportation Fund in place to enable western suppliers and producers to make bids on those projects.
Not once since 1984 when the Government began to administer the Act has it made any effort to hold the railways accountable for that responsibility, to ask the CNR and CPR to what extent they are sourcing in western Canada and to what degree they are buying their goods and services in western Canada, or to use the sanction in the Bill which is that if they do not do that the Crow benefit can be withheld.
That is the kind of tough action on behalf of western Canada that one would expect from a Government which says it believes in western Canada. The Government has never done that. If you look at the records you will see that neither the previous Minister nor the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) ever set that as a priority. Instead the Government was piecing out the Western Industrial Transportation Fund in small projects across the West. The fund was retained, so the Conservatives must have thought it was a good idea, but they did not use it for its purpose which was to ensure that we would have a synergy between railway investment and sourcing which would have given western businesses an opportunity to move into a new area of activity. That is once again an opportunity lost. If the Minister says that that will now be a responsibility of the new agency, that is fine, but that has not happened over the past three years.
That is what I mean by an entitlement, the requirement to ensure that the federal Government, which has very large resources to invest in education, research, and procurement, ensures that there is a fair sharing. That must be done because at the present time there is not fair sharing. The record of federal procurement still is that 80 per cent of it takes place within the Montreal-Ottawa-Toronto triangle. It takes almost an affirmative action for western Canada and Atlantic Canada to change that around. That is the kind of political muscle and political priority which we would expect from this agency. However, I did not hear the Minister talking about that. I did not hear him say that that is what this new agency will do.
I would even suggest that moving the agency out of the capital of Canada, away from the action, will make it less effective in getting the influence and making the case that has to be made on a day-by-day basis. In running a government it is the small details that count, the paper that comes across your desk every day and the access you have to other Departments. You have to be there to make yourself heard, to make your influence felt.
Western Economic Diversification Act
It may be that by detaching this agency it will lose its ability to make an impact, to make a strong political statement day by day, hour by hour, in this capital, which needs to be done in order not to lose the decisions on contracts, research, and grants which take place in Ottawa on a daily basis. In fact, the organizational base that has been constructed may be weakening the ability of western Canada to get the entitlement that it needs. That may in fact be the problem that we are facing in terms of this kind of organization.
There is less money than was put in before, there is a questionable level of co-ordination, and there is certainly less influence at Cabinet level. A number of things have already been cancelled and taken away which are not being replaced. Most important, there is no blueprint, no vision. There is no compelling set of priorities for western Canada which can be responded to. It does not have to be unilateral or arbitrary, but it should set out what must be done.
Only the federal Government has the capacity to do that at the regional level. It is very hard to get the Premier of Alberta to speak up for the Province of Manitoba. Certainly we have never seen that, as evidenced in the CF-18 case. However, because the federal Government represents a larger jurisdiction it should represent a larger vision. It should use its capacity as a national Government to set forward those kinds of priorities and ensure that they are implemented and organized on a regional level.
There is no such aspiration or sense of objective, which is so essential if western Canada is going to keep pace. I return to the basic point that we have seen in this country in the last three or four years a highly unequal, unfair level of growth. If you look at the growth rates in Canada you will see that the concentration of economic activity, jobs, investment, and placement has taken place in the central regions of Canada.
I am not arguing with those regions, but I am saying that it has increased the disparity. It is making the gap grow wider. To arrest that will take a very singular and strong-minded federal government setting out a whole new set of objectives and priorities for the regions.
That is not what we have had, that is not what we are receiving. The IRDP has been cancelled. It runs out in June. One of the important tools of the direct grants industry will cease to operate in June, and there is no sign that the federal Government intends to replace it. There have been major cutbacks in programs that the regions need; support in the fishing industry, in agriculture, and in research. There have been cutbacks in education and in major areas in which the regions have been able to develop specialized programs. If we allow that to continue the gap will grow wider and wider.
The only organization that has the ability to stop that and rewrite the balance is the federal Government, in effect the Parliament of Canada. The philosophy behind this measure is

March 1, 1988
Adjournment Debate
not the way it will happen. It is effectively separating the regions in trying to deal with the problem in isolation.
I would be much more supportive of a strong, effective department of regional industrial development which had a firm mandate, with real resources and a Minister that had real clout, rather than the fumbling Ministers we have seen in the last three or four years. We need a Department and a Minister that could exercise that kind of influence in Ottawa to ensure that the priorities set for the regions at the national level would be carried out with effectiveness and efficiency.
Much like a centrifugal force, if Canada is left to its market forces, and, in some cases, to its natural forces, it will tend to separate into fragments because the central agencies cannot hold it together. Generations of federal Governments have had the responsibility to try to control that centrifugal force through coherent leadership and direction from the central part of the country in terms of the national Government.
I submit that this program will not accomplish that goal or provide those opportunities. Western diversification is one of the most important issues in Canada in light of the problems I have already enunciated. If we allow the condition of native people in western Canada to deteriorate any further, we will face one of the most serious condemnations in our history. Canadians must come to grips with this issue.
We cannot allow the regions to become further alienated so that westerners increasingly feel they can no longer trust their national Government or federal institutions. This is already happening according to a survey last summer which showed that 30 per cent or 40 per cent of westerners would be prepared to vote for a western separatist Party. One hardly wants to see such a condition enhanced.
I believe this issue requires much more thought and creative ability than we see in this western diversification program. This is far more motivated by the political concerns of the Government rather than the national concerns. That is why I believe it is very important that we must and will have a new kind of western development program when a new government takes office in a very short period of time.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of Western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
Madam Speaker, are there not questions and comments at this point?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
When the Bill is
first brought forward for second reading, the first three Members to speak are allowed 40 minutes. There are no questions or comments following those speeches.

Madam Speaker, I believe the principles of the department we are discussing are certainly supported by all Members of the House and people in western Canada. The principles are that we have an office that will attempt to diversify the economy of western Canada. This is something we have needed for many years.
As well, coming from my populist CCF roots, I am a strong believer in the need for more decentralization in this country to allow local people more input into decisions that affect their lives and their communities. I certainly support those two principles which are very important in the establishment of this office.
The first requirement in order to make those principles work is money. While I suppose every Minister will agree that they do not have enough money, my concern as a western Member of Parliament is that there may not be enough money in the program to make it effective.
Many other government programs have been cancelled, to be rolled into this particular department. The Minister tells us that there is $1.2 billion over five years, which is roughly $60 million per province per year. I recognize that he is treating the West as one region rather than four provinces, but it still works out to $60 million per year per province.
Furthermore, there is a debate about how much of that is new money and how much is old money. I am sure different economists will give different opinions, that the Government will say it is mostly new money, and many others will say it is primarily recycled money from existing programs.
March 1, 1988

The former Finance Minister in the Government of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who just spoke, announced the Western Development Fund in the amount of some $4 billion at that time. When one compares the $4 billion in 1980, which was spent over some four years, with $1.2 billion, it is not very much, even if it is new money.
I have said privately and publicly that the Minister is one of the more competent and sincere Ministers in the Cabinet. I am sure he will do a good job with what he has. I sincerely hope that this particular office is more than just the western Conservative political office in anticipation of the approaching election, and that it will really mean something and develop into a meaningful institution.
My friend from Winnipeg mentioned in closing the problem of western separatism and alienation. He referred to a poll in which a large number of western Canadians would consider voting for a western independence or separatist Party in certain circumstances.
This debate is crucial because it is important that western Canadians be not misled and that the office being established will diversify the economy in western Canada. It is important that it be an office that is funded with a meaningful amount of new money. If not, it will only add to the western alienation that already exists.
We know about westerners turning to new political forces. That is how my Party began, with the CCF and Tommy Douglas many years ago. That is where a certain brand of the Conservative Party began, with John Diefenbaker in the 1940s and 1950s in Saskatchewan and across the Prairies. There is the Social Credit Party, which arose with western populism, and the western Canada concept. We now see Preston Manning's Reform Party in western Canada.
There is a significant feeling in western Canada that we have not received our fair share from Confederation. The worst that could happen is to have a new and promising department with a promising Minister which does not deliver in the way western Canadians believe it should.
The program before us today had several false starts over the last year or so. It was formally announced last August by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he spoke in the City of Edmonton, Alberta. It was unveiled about three weeks before the Government had tabled in this House two studies detailing the reasons for a $79 million overrun at the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. I am sure you recall that overrun, Madam Speaker, in the Department of the former Minister, the then Hon. Member for Longueuil who is no longer in Cabinet.
We have also seen since this Government took office a tremendous cut-back in regional and economic development spending. In 1984 the Government spent some $14.8 billion on economic and regional development. The Estimates for 1987
Western Economic Diversification Act
were cutback to $11.8 billion. There is a cut-back of around $3 billion which is a very big drop. In its place, we have the western diversification office, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, and FEDNOR which is the equivalent in northern Ontario.
I really wonder whether or not, when all the calculations are in, these new agencies will actually have as much money to spend as the old regional development program itself. As I have said, there is a certain amount of deja vu. I mentioned the Liberal Western Development Fund in 1980 of some $4 billion. I have also mentioned the fact that that was more money at that time than in our Budget today. In many cases, even that $4 billion is a bit of a phantom fund in terms of where all that extra money went. There are some more similarities. The bureaucratic head of the Liberal Western Development Fund was a gentleman named Bruce Rawson. After spending some time at the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, he has now taken up Deputy Minister duties at the Edmonton headquarters of the western diversification office.
I have already mentioned the fact that there is some $1.2 billion allocated to this particular department. There is a debate as to what is new and what is old. That is a very interesting debate because what we should be emphasizing here is that there are three program instruments, once the responsibility of DRIE that have ended or are about to end in the very near future. The first program is the Industrial Research and Development Program, IRDP, which will terminate in June of 1988. The lesser known program is the Western Transportation and Industrial Development Program, WTIDP. That is now finished but there are several ongoing projects which are funded fifty-fifty. The third program is the Economic and Regional Development Agreements, ERDA. These agreements expire in 1989 and 1990.
The Western Transportation and Industrial Development Program was re-jigged, in a sense, to become the western diversification office's main funding instrument, known as the Western Economic Diversification Program. Some of the ERDA agreements are the responsibility of Departments such as the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Science and Technology, Transport Canada, and so on. In other cases, the responsibility formerly with DRIE is transferred to the western diversification office. You can see, Madam Speaker, that the other programs that were there at one time will now no longer be in place.
The Minister stated in the House today a number of the purposes for the western diversification office and for the Bill before the House today. The Prime Minister himself, when he made the announcement, stated the mandate of the western diversification office. First it was important we have an office to co-ordinate and communicate all federal programs and activities that contribute to the economic development and diversification of the West. Second, the program will support business infrastructure to further the economic development and diversification of the western economy. Third, the office

March 1, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
will undertake activities that will facilitate the creation of new enterprises and business consistent with our evolving international treaty policy. Fourth, it will represent the interests of western Canada in the development of national policies and the design of national programs to ensure that western Canada is effectively linked to decision-making in Ottawa. Those are the four things the Prime Minister spoke about, and the Minister also mentioned them earlier on this afternoon.
While the western diversification office views itself as a funder of last resort, its most interesting role is that of coordinator of federal programming in western Canada. Considering the important presence of larger and more powerful Departments such as the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of Transport and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in the West, the co-ordinator function will take considerable determination by the Minister and his Deputy. It is easier to imagine these Departments locked in a tense policy struggle with the western diversification office, and with the western diversification losing in the end despite the good intentions of the Minister or the Deputy Minister.
This will be a small department without the clout of the Department of Finance, for example. There is a dispute taking place right now with respect to interest rates where the Bank of Canada is saying that interest rates should not come down because the economy is overheated in southern Ontario. I argue that interest rates in western Canada should come down because when interest rates are high they tend to drive up the Canadian dollar and make it more difficult for us to export to the United States. What kind of clout will this Minister have in his new department when it comes to arguing with the Department of Finance, with the Minister in charge of Energy, Mines and Resources or the Minister of Agriculture or, indeed, with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans? The Minister suggests that his regional department will be guiding the expenditures of departmental A bases. That will be quite an accomplishment given the eminence of the Departments I have already mentioned. Therefore, I am not sure what influence, in the final analysis, this department will have, particularly when the headquarters of the new department will be in Edmonton rather than in the City of Ottawa where there would be contact with other key policy makers in the normal course of duties.
Another role of the western diversification office is to act as a "pathfinder" which ties in with the role of being a "funder of last resort", and the Minister referred to that earlier. When a prospective applicant for funding arrives at one of the four western diversification offices, the first thing the officers will do is to determine whether or not the project can be dealt with by another funding agency or department. In other words, the first thing they will look for is a way to refer the applicant to another department or to another agency. It appears that only after an applicant has exhausted all other avenues, will the western diversification office step in and consider being a funder of last resort.
Judging from the projects announced thus far, and many offers have been made, as the Minister has announced in the House and elsewhere, the small and medium-sized businesses can take little comfort in the trend. Perhaps it is only a trend. I am not sure whether this will be the record after two or three years. So far, there does not seem to be much of a bias towards smaller and medium-sized businesses by this particular department. By way of example, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business expressed considerable exasperation with the western diversification office.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business is not exactly a radical socialist organization. It is a fairly conservative institution, as the Minister himself would agree. There have been many big ticket projects announced, including some which ought to have been funded through normal departmental spending, for example, millions of dollars for a salmon enhancement program that ought to have been funded through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in a regular departmental budget. Perhaps the Minister at some time will explain why this particular program, costing millions of dollars, was funded through the western diversification office.
The title of this Bill is the Western Economic Diversification Act. Some of the programs funded so far do not have anything to do with diversification. They are for development. We have nothing against development, but it seems to me that the main purpose here is to diversify the western economy. Perhaps the salmon program should have been an ongoing development program, funded through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
There are two notable large private sector projects that leave some people in western Canada wondering. The American-owned B.F. Goodrich company picked up some $418,000 for a project that would create no new jobs at the plant. This is money that it states will maintain existing jobs. The press release itself stated that there would be the creation of no new jobs in this particular case.
In addition, the second largest pulp and paper company in Japan will benefit from a $9.5 million contribution from the western diversification office. This is the second largest plant in Japan in the pulp and paper business. One might have expected that these huge companies could have generated their own funds internally or could have borrowed money from the banks or financial institutions, but that was not the case. On the one hand, it is B.F. Goodrich, and on the other hand it is Daishowa, the second largest pulp and paper company in Japan.
Perhaps it is only circumstance that in these first announcements some money has gone to large foreign-based companies. But it is a bit of a trend-setter that has many westerners in small and medium-sized business concerned about the priorities of the Government across the way.
March 1, 1988

It might also be suggested that $9.5 million that was offered to the shakes and shingles industry was to make up for past transgressions of the Minister of International Trade (Ms. Carney). There was the dispute in the shakes and shingles industry where the Minister of International Trade was on the hot seat in terms of how she had handled that portfolio vis-avis the forest industry in British Columbia. The Fraser Valley Independent Shakes and Shingles Producers Association is receiving the $9.5 million to attempt to put up U.S. demand for its products. All this is after that controversial tariff that was in place.
Since the outset of the program there have been complaints from many observers, and some people say most observers, that $1.2 billion over five years is a very small amount of money. I know that there have been complaints about this, and earlier I referred to the fact that it works out to approximately $60 million per province per year divided between the four western provinces.
The Premier of Manitoba has stated that Manitoba should be receiving some more money. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has been quoted in the newspapers in Manitoba as stating that he supports the Premier of Manitoba and that Manitoba should receive around $300 million as its share.
If one looks at the projects approved from August 4, 1987 up to February 22, 1988, in a survey of the four offices, there have been projects worth $275.8 million allocated for expenditure. Using the information that we have, we find out that Manitoba appears to be losing the race. British Columbia has received commitments for $152 million; my province of Saskatchewan is not doing too badly with commitments of $95 million; Alberta has received commitments of $22 million; and Manitoba has received commitments of $6.8 million.
I suppose that is why the Minister of National Health and Welfare is a little concerned, and why Premier Pawley is rightfully concerned, about the moneys allocated. 1 am sure that the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay) will rise in the House in the next couple of days and say that he too is concerned about the fact that Manitoba is thus far on the lower end of the scale.
I know that the Minister across the way is treating the West as one region, but even although he treats it as one region he must be very careful that there is equity between the provinces and equity between the regions within the region of western Canada. There are varying unemployment levels and varying needs from one province to the other, and indeed within the provinces. A concern that a number of people have is where the funding and the money is going.
Is the western diversification office going to be a vehicle for patronage? In 1984 the Prime Minister stated that it was only the Liberal Party that exercised this terrible thing called patronage, and that he would end that particular practice. Since the Prime Minister took office there has been an awful lot of patronage handed out to the friends of the Prime
Western Economic Diversification Act
Minister and other people in the Cabinet of the Conservative Party that sits across the way.
In this particular case there is no board of directors dominated by Tory appointees, as is the case with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. However, a noted friend of the Tory Government, a gentleman named Michael Walker of the Vancouver-based Fraser Institute, stated, "Unfortunately the way they're going to spend it will be determined by political interests, not economic interests . .. the reason they're doing this is not to improve the western economy, but to improve their political fortunes".
That was stated by a friend of the Conservative Party in the Fraser Institute. I wish to point out that there is always a danger here that there could be considerable political patronage.
I wish to return to the $1.2 billion. I said it was very important that, if we do have a diversification office, it diversifies the economy of western Canada and it also has enough money to make it meaningful and significant for western Canadians.
Recently, when discussing the $1.2 billion, the current Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) stated, "It sounds like a lot of money, but in the over-all scheme of things it is not that great". I suppose you often hear, Madam Speaker, Members of Parliament saying that they need more money or more funding.
I remember the time when many years before I was elected to this place C.D. Howe lost the election to Doug Fisher in Thunder Bay when he rose in the House and said, "What is a million?" But $1.2 billion in western Canada over five years is not that much money, particularly because a lot of it is not new money. The Minister in charge of Grains and Oilseeds and in charge of the Wheat Board has stated, "It sounds like a lot of money, but in the over-all scheme of things it is not that great".
A Financial Post editorial stated, "... There is no doubt whatever that the potential contribution of Ottawa's western diversification initiative is truly piddling. Fifty million dollars per province per year won't diversify very much".
One of the more prominent members of the Conservative Party, the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), when speaking to the Downtown Rotary Club of Edmonton stated, "The recently announced western diversification strategy, though inadequate in its funding, is certainly a modest step in the right direction". The Hon. Member talks about it being "modest", going in the "right direction", but certainly "inadequate in its funding".
Frank Came, a senior officer with the western diversification Ottawa office, stated, "The fund is not all that big when you look at the amount of capital".

March 1, 1988
Montreal Gulf Refinery
I wish to return to the Hon. Member for Edmonton- Strathcona. When he left the Conservative caucus approximately one year ago, one reason for doing so was his impatience with the Government's launching of the western diversification office. The following was written by the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona in 1981 in response to the Liberal Western Development Fund. "The sending of Bruce Rawson to Edmonton as the federal Government's senior adviser on Western Canadian affairs will be seen by many westerners as another in a long series of gimmicks from a regime which sees our region primarily as a convenient whipping boy in an attempt to shore up political support elsewhere".

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT IMPORTANCE OF SAVING GULF OIL REFINERY
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT IMPORTANCE OF SAVING GULF OIL REFINERY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of intervening in the matter of the Gulf refinery of Montreal East in order to save the hundreds of jobs which are threatened and to protect Quebec consumers, thus respecting the unanimous resolution of the National Assembly of Quebec.
He said: Madam Speaker, first of all, I realize it seems a bit odd to be talking about the Gulf refinery today. However, we must not forget I put this motion on the Order Paper on October 1, 1986, and that despite the delay, and in the present circumstances, the problems of the petrochemical industry in Montreal East and what remains of the Gulf refinery are still very much with us.
I would like to start by providing some background to explain the reasons for this motion. First of all, all the facilities belonging to Gulf Canada had been purchased by Petro-Canada, and this included all refinery and service operations, all facilities located in Ontario, Western Canada and Quebec.
The House may recall that the Reichmann brothers and the Atlantic provinces had decided to sell the refinery and service station operations because, according to our information, the Conservative Government did not want Petro-Canada to invest more in upgrading these operations. Now, following the
purchase proposals, another company, Ultramar, announced it would buy all installations in Quebec and the Maritimes, with the admitted intention-this is a British company-of closing down the Gulf refinery operations in Montreal's east end, while maintaining service operations. Gaz Metropolitan was bidding on the same installations, but unlike Ultramar, it intended to continue to operate the Gulf refinery as well as the service stations.
Under the rules of Investment Canada, the Conservative version of FIRA, Ultramar, as a foreign company, required the Government's authorization to purchase the Gulf refinery. We know that the Minister at the time, and Cabinet, in full possession of the facts, agreed. However, this was not what the National Assembly and most groups wanted, and at the time, several Conservative Members resigned to make the federal Government say no to Ultramar, because it had the power to do so, and I think it had a duty to say no to Ultramar, which was a foreign company. If two Canadian companies had been involved, the Conservative Government could hardly have been blamed for acting the way it did, because it did not have the power to prevent normal competition and thus would not have been responsible for the consequences.
But in view of the fact that a foreign company had to have Cabinet approval, and this is unfortunate, at that point there has even been Conservative Ministers who supposedly resigned over that. But that is not the important point to recall, in my view. It is rather the fact that at the time, the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) on the Conservative side, who was Minister of Transport, stated that people in Cabinet, people in caucus and the Ministers when they gave that approval lacked important information. That statement did not come from a Liberal, or an NDP, or a labour leader-it was made by someone in Cabinet, who had access to information and who blamed her colleagues for blindly approving, and we know very well that it has been proven there was a lack of refining capability in Quebec and there were surpluses across Canada.
But it must be stated today that while there were 450 employees at that time, that company has now been converted to Kemtec and there are now 250 employees, and if that industry was not completely shut down it is thanks to the representatives of the Gulf refinery employees, that is the former refinery, Messrs. Chouinard, Baril and Tremblay who never stopped fighting. At the time they got involved, they formed a coalition and so on. It will be remembered that the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) came to make a show, by signing the petition ... he would not sign it in front of the cameras for fear of his Leader-he wanted to have a cake and eat it too.
But we succeeded in saving the industry, thanks to the actions of the Quebec Energy Minister, Mr. Caccia, and the Bourassa Government, with Lavalin corporation, to ensure that the company would be saved, and today there are 250 jobs, there is no more refining work done and consumers are not protected. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is indeed regrettable that the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) insists on taking up valuable House time to respond to an old problem that no longer exists. The closure of the Montreal Gulf refinery in 1986 did not and will not lead to problems with refining capacity in Quebec. Closure of the refinery did not lead to high prices for gasoline or home heating oil. As my hon. colleague has pointed out to the House, the rationalization of the industry in the middle of this decade did not create problems. On the contrary, conditions have improved.
After the Gulf closure, refining capacity, in fact, was close to being on balance with internal oil product requirements, and the province even developed a small surplus capacity as Quebec oil consumption continued to fall. This, of course, was directly due-and I must give credit where it is due-to the former Government's off-oil and conservation programs which

March 1, 1988
Montreal Gulf Refinery
we have continued. The fortunate fact remains, however, that Quebec has continued to enjoy a state of surplus capacity since the refinery closure.
My hon. colleague, the Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce), noted earlier that the closure had no effect whatsoever on the price of gasoline and home heating oil in Quebec. Gasoline prices, after deducting provincial taxes, are within five cents of the Canadian average. Home heating oil prices, with or without Quebec's provincial tax, are significantly below those in Toronto and Maritime cities.
The situation with independent retailers has improved immensely. The number of outlets operated by independents climbed from 256 in December, 1984, to 331 in 1988. The independents' market share also increased. In Montreal their share of retail motor gasoline sales rose from 13.4 per cent at the end of 1984 to 16.7 per cent in early 1988. This shows that consumers in Quebec have been well served and should continue to enjoy the benefits of free market prices and the competition which dictates oil product price levels.
The industry itself has also acted in a responsible manner in utilizing the components of the former Gulf refinery. Lavalin bought and recommissioned the Gulf facilities to produce petrochemicals. Bitumen bought the asphalt plant and resumed asphalt operations. Together with Shell's new catalytic cracker in Montreal and Petro-Canada's total residual oil "cat-cracking" unit, it is evident that the industry in Quebec, like the Government of Canada, is committed to efficiency and flexibility. They are well positioned to adapt to changing market conditions from which both consumers and industry can benefit.
You have the facts, Madam Speaker, on the healthy situation in Quebec, but there is another related area which is sometimes misunderstood when talking about Quebec's energy situation, that is, the question of security of supply. What would happen if Quebec's supplies were disrupted? Although this event is unlikely, it would not be prudent to dismiss completely the possibility of a short-term disruption. Ample surplus refining capacity exists in Ontario and the Atlantic provinces to meet any temporary interruption in Quebec supplies. Aside from Quebec's surplus capacity of 42,000 barrels a day in 1986, the Atlantic provinces enjoyed a surplus of 85,000 barrels and Ontario a surplus of 124,000 barrels.
Other contingency plans could also be implemented immediately, such as accelerated use of existing stocks. These inventories at the refinery and wholesale levels could be replenished within a few days using rail or truck deliveries from adjacent provinces. In addition, stocks could be imported from the United States and Europe in a week or two. The impact of a short-term supply disruption of inventories at the retail level would probably be marginal, if any. I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that the industry, if ever faced with higher than average depletion rates from its storage facilities, would take the necessary corrective action to avert any supply tightness at the retail level.
Although a temporary supply rupture would result in a mild price hike, little likelihood exists of consumers going without oil. Suppliers will incur almost any cost to ensure that customers are not lost because of a temporary slow-down of product delivery.
In addition, the reduction in refinery capacity due to equipment failure or operating problems can also be off set by the ability of refineries to operate in excess of their rated capacities for sustained periods. In western Canada, for example, refineries have often run at 103 to 120 per cent of rated capacity for several months during periods of refinery expansions and additions.
It is clear to me that, in view of the available alternatives to meet supply contingencies, maintenance of surplus refinery capacity in Quebec is an unnecessary and expensive insurance premium.
The Government's contingency plans are not limited to domestic disruption. Canada's membership in the International Energy Agency, an autonomous organization within the organization of economic co-operation and development, further enhances the collective energy and economic security of Canada and its major trading partners. The 21 member participating countries have agreed to an emergency oil sharing system and to reduce dependence on oil imports through conservation, energy research and development, and the development of alternative energy sources.
The International Energy Agency is committed to determining requirements for an embargo on one or more IEA member countries and minimizing the adverse economic impacts arising from an international oil supply disruption.
Member countries are asked to maintain emergency reserves equal to 90 days of net imports-from which Canada is exempt, being a net exporter-to have ready emergency programs which would reduce consumption by at least 7 per cent, and to participate in the equitable sharing of available supplies.
In addition, Madam Speaker, Canada actively participates in an allocation supply test conducted by all IEA member countries every three years. The sixth such international test, called AST6, will be conducted from October 1 to November 30 of this year. The exercise tests the supply sharing and allocation mechanisms of each member country to ensure that each member can react quickly, efficiently, and judiciously in an international emergency.
The test scenario asks each country to establish, first, its domestic needs, and then to determine what it can give up for those countries that have less supply. Each country cuts back equally and shares equitably the available surplus. The worst case international scenario, for example, a total cut-off from Middle East sources, would precipitate no more than a 10 per cent depletion in supply. I submit, therefore, to the Hon. excess refining capacity, its lower dependence on oil and oil products compared with neighbouring provinces, its abundant hydro electrical and alternative energy sources, and its proximity to neighbouring supplies rule out any major inconvenience to consumers in times of a short or even longterm supply disruption, either domestic or international.
