Madam Speaker, on February 23, I asked the Prime Minister a question about the division in his party on Bill C-72, an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada.
First, I should point out that this Bill is now before Parliament and that, up to date, it has been the subject of a very short debate. The only leader of a political party to speak in this debate has been the Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner), who spoke on February 9, and I wish to congratulate him on his intervention, especially as he was Minister of Justice when the original Act was passed in 1969, and, in this capacity, be piloted the initial version of the Official Languages Act.
He is the only party leader to have spoken in the current debate in support of this very important piece of legislation.
I would like to remind the House of what he said at the time:
March 1, 1988

-I believe that now the time is right to proceed to consolidate and enhance the Official Languages Act. Now is the time to weave in the many advances made since 1969 to keep the Act abreast of a changing mood and a positive tolerance in Canada. Therefore, the time is right.
The Leader of the Opposition also said, and I quote:
We cannot proclaim equality and then simply let it happen by accident. We must adjust our laws to accepted constitutional principles. The laws of this country must accord with the Constitution. That is a primary impetus behind bringing this law up to date.
One of the reasons why we Liberals support this Bill is that it is part of a very long tradition of our party. We introduced the 1969 legislation and we naturally observed what happened between 1969 and 1984. We were the instigators of the statement by the House of Commons in 1973 and of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms of 1982, and under the able chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), we supported the work of the Joint Committee on Official Languages between 1980 and 1984.
The Liberal Party has always considered bilingualism to be the corner stone of our electoral and political programs.
I must say that the position of the Conservative Party has changed over the years. I recognize that more and more Members of the Conservative Party accept and recognize the importance of bilinguism in Canada. There are quite a few Members representing various areas in this country, whether Quebec, the Maritimes, Ontario and even Western Canada, who can now speak both official languages, and I am quite pleased to say that the Conservative Cabinet is now made up of Anglophone Ministers who can speak French very well.
Unfortunately, there still remains a significant pocket of resistance, the BBC within the Conservative Party. And even if the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister try to minimize this resistance, there is no doubt, as reported in Maclean's, that there are bones of contention. And I quote:
With respect to the language revolt, as Maclean's cited, there is a profound difference of opinion between the Hon. Member for Winnipeg Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) and the Hon. Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy), who have very strong views, on the one hand, while the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) and the Hon. Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon) have expressed a different point of view.
Probably more eloquently than any other group, the Winnipeg Free Press expressed this division when it stated:
The revisions to Bill C-72 which the anti-bilingual (Tory) caucus asked for this week would make English the language of federal civil service offices in all parts of Canada except New Brunswick and part of Quebec.
The article in the Winnipeg Free Press further stated:
This proposal is insulting to French-speaking people who rightly regard their language as being every bit as good as Mr. McKenzie's and worthy of equal treatment in the federal administration . . .
Adjournment Debate
Language policy for Canada can be discussed in rational terms. Emotion is always present in the debate about clan symbols but the duty of responsible political leaders is to appeal as little as possible to hatred and as much as possible to reason. Proposing to stamp out the use of French in wide sections of the federal public service is such an appeal to communal hostility. The Mulroney Government should make clear in all parts of Canada that it will not for a moment entertain such insulting proposals and will not join in playing the game of clan hatreds.

It is clear, in my opinion, that the Prime Minister should imitate his predecessor and indicate to the Members of his Party that bilingualism is a fundamental policy of his Party and that, as Mr. Stanfield had refused Mayor Jones as a Conservative candidate, the Prime Minister, faced with the Opposition of a number of his own Members, should clearly indicate to them that they will not be able to be candidates under the Conservative ticket during the next election if they do not support the Government's policy on bilingualism.

AND POLICY/CAPE BRETON DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION

Mr. Speaker, on February 23 I raised in the House of Commons my concerns about the funding and policy of the Government of Canada with regard to the Cape Breton Development Corporation. This issue is not something new that I have brought to the attention of the Government. I have been bringing the matter to its attention for quite some time.
I was somewhat concerned and disappointed with the Estimates tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Equally so I was concerned and once again expressed the view that the commitment of the Government of Canada to the coalfields in eastern Nova Scotia left a lot to be desired.
It has been clear from the outset that there is a bias against the facilitation of and indeed assistance to the coal industry in my province. Some years ago a former Premier of my province initiated a policy which indicated that Nova Scotians, as their energy policy, would utilize coal from eastern Nova Scotia to produce electricity for their homes and businesses. It has been a difficult task for many workers involved in the coal industry to sustain a reasonable and viable living in order to provide for their families.
Early on in the administration of the Government, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) took it upon himself to initiate a committee to look at the possibility of utilizing Canadian coal in Ontario Hydro. I have asked the Minister repeatedly to include representations from Atlantic Canada, in particular eastern Nova Scotia. To date that request has fallen on deaf ears, and there has been no action from the Government of Canada.
Coal miners in Cape Breton would dearly love to have the opportunity to provide their particular product to the Nova Scotia Power Corporation at a fair and reasonable price. They would also like to have similar opportunities to the ones which seem to be given to coalfields in western Canada in order to supply coal to Ontario Hydro. I would have hoped that the Minister, and in particular the Deputy Prime Minister, would have been able to see the importance of having that particular
matter addressed in a positive way. Instead, that has not been the case.
With regard to the Estimates provided by the Government, no new moneys are being provided to the coal industry. What we see is a Government which is following through on a promise and commitment made by my Government in 1984. At that time, because of a tragic fire in the coalfields, a coal mine went out of existence, namely, No. 26 Colliery. My Government committed in excess of $200 million for what is known as the "Lingan Phalen".
We do not see any new commitments. We do not see any new moneys whatsoever in the Estimates for this year or for last year for the expansion of the coal industry on the Island of Cape Breton. It is a cornerstone industry, not only of Cape Breton Island, but of the Province of Nova Scotia. It is Nova Scotia's largest employer. It provides an economic spin-off second to none in the Atlantic region.
We have a Government which does not want to commit itself to the expansion of the coal industry. The idea that miners are supposed to go a mile or two underneath the ground, seven miles out underneath the ocean floor and merely reap the product from underground, take it out, ship it domestically or abroad, must come to an end. A new thinking, a new approach must be put in place. They have to get that product and they have to redefine the product in Nova Scotia in order to find more jobs so that it will be environmentally acceptable domestically as well as internationally.
In the Estimates there is no new money, none whatsoever to address that fundamental concern that all of us have in Cape Breton about our cornerstone industry. Union representatives, time after time after time, have impressed upon local provincial and national authorities that a clear unequivocal commitment was needed for our coal industry. The Estimates do not provide that, Madam Speaker.
Probably weeks prior to a federal election we will have the Minister responsible roll into the island of Cape Breton with a piece of paper saying "Now we are committed to the coal industry", and announce expenditures that may take place years and years ahead. But those expenditures are not in the Estimates, Madam Speaker, nor were they in last year's Estimates as to what the Government believes and where it wants to take the coal industry. It leaves many in my constituency, and certainly within the coal industry, suspicious, apprehensive and concerned about the future of that industry.
I say that with great sincerity for we have witnessed in recent years the gutting of in excess of 600 jobs in the Cape Breton Development Corporation. That is a very serious matter.
I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary today will give us more information with regard to new dollars for the expansion of the coal industry in a variety of ways, many of which he already knows because he has heard me announce them. I hope he addresses the issue of why we in eastern Nova Scotia cannot
March 1, 1988

be part and parcel of the committee which was struck by the Deputy Prime Minister.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not know what it is like at your home. As you know, I have not been over to visit. However, if you came to visit my house, you would find that I have two really magnificent maple trees on the front lawn of my house.
I do not want you to get the impression that those are the only trees that I have around my home because I have a lot of them. I have some beautiful spruce trees, a sumac tree and cedar trees. We used to have an ash tree and an elm tree before they died and had to be taken down. We have a lot of trees around our home, but the two that 1 am really proud of, the trees I have a real feeling for, are these two magnificent maple trees.
My house is on a corner, the corner of McRae Drive and Hanna Road. One of these maple trees is on the front lawn on the McRae Drive side of the house right in front of our big living-room bay window. This is a wonderful tree. The house was built in about 1937 and the tree has probably been there for about that long. It has a lot of character. It has a bit of a lean, of course. There are squirrels living in that tree and it is just a wonderful tree.
On the Hanna Road side of our house, up in front of one of the bedrooms, there is another tree. That tree has not been there for quite as long, but it is a big, mature tree as well. I really have a lot of feeling for those trees, but both trees have a problem.
Every year in the spring, the leaves burst out and they mature, but around the beginning of July recently, those leaves have started to shrivel up and die. After they shrivel up and die, they fall off. They look terrible, the trees look terrible and it is a real tragedy.
I wonder to myself what is the cause of what is happening to those trees. Some people say it is acid rain. That may very well be the case, I am not sure. I have a neighbour down the street, Jim Hannah, who is a tree lover. He tells me that my trees and perhaps hundreds and maybe even thousands of others in our neighbourhood will die. He cannot say for sure that the reason is acid rain, but that is a good probability.
Even if it is not acid rain that is causing the leaves on my trees to shrivel up and apparently die, we know that acid rain has to be stopped. It is our job and the Government's job to stop acid rain because that is what the people of this country expect us to do.
I know as well that for the first time in the history of Canada, our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has put acid rain on the agenda as a top priority in discussions with the United States and has made an enormous effort to make progress in having the Americans reduce their acid rain emissions. This is

March 1, 1988
Adjournment Debate
the first time that this effort has been put forward by a Canadian Prime Minister.
We know as well that we simply cannot force the Americans to cut acid rain emissions. The United States is a free and independent country. We are not going to go to war with the Americans and start shooting at them. Some people think we would not be able to beat them anyway. Regardless, we know that if the Americans will not agree to cut their acid rain emissions, we will not be able to do it for them and we will not be able to force them to do it.
At the same time, we have been trying to cut domestic acid rain emissions. We have agreements with all the eastern provinces to cut acid rain emissions by some 50 per cent by 1994. As the Parliamentary Secretary said, we are putting our money where our mouth is. There is a commitment of some $335 million on the part of the Government to help reduce acid rain emissions domestically here in Canada.

Now the U.S. comes along and says that is not a real commitment to cut acid rain emissions in Canada by 50 per cent. It is only 35 per cent. On top of that The Toronto Star has agreed with them editorially and says the Government is trying to mislead us. I think that is a bunch of baloney. You know and I know that the U.S. is always trying one way or another to weasel out of its commitment to cut acid rain. As far as The Toronto Star is concerned, this Government could raise the old age pension 1,000 per cent or 1 million per cent and we would still be criticized. I just hope its readers take those criticisms with a grain of salt.
It does not matter to me or to you, and 1 know it does not matter to the Parliamentary Secretary, what the Americans think or, for that matter, whether The Toronto Star agrees with them or not on this issue. speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-PLAN TO REDUCE EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say first that I thought the Hon. Member was advertising the sale of his house, but I know he wants to remain in the great riding of York East. It was a great introduction to his question which we wish to respond to in a more comprehensive way.
Canada set a clear, straightforward objective of solving this problem of damage caused by acid rain. To protect the Canadian environment, acid fall-out in all vulnerable areas must be reduced to less than 20 kilograms per hectare per year. We have found that damage occurs when the acid fallout is above this number. We also have evidence that when acid fall-out drops below this threshold, recovery of the
environment starts to take place. I visited the University of Toronto yesterday and its Environmental Studies Institute, and indeed they are finding some evidence in the Sudbury area of recovery starting to take place.
We have gone through the calculations to tell us how many tonnes of sulphur dioxide can be released into the atmosphere and from what areas in order to achieve the 20 kilogram per hectare objective. We have concluded two things. First, total annual sulphur dioxide emissions from the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border eastward must be reduced to 2.3 million tonnes, or about 50 per cent of the emissions allowed in 1980. Second, the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide from the U.S. into eastern Canada must be reduced by about two million tonnes per year. Again, about 50 per cent of the 1980 level.
Canada is well on the way to delivering what it has to. More than 90 per cent of the emission reductions required to get down to the 2.3 million tonne level are in regulatory or program form and have been formally ratified in federal-provincial agreements. All seven eastern provinces have now signed agreements. That is a great credit to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), indeed to our Government. Under the program, the necessary emission reductions will be achieved by 1994 at the latest. Currently, eastern Canadian sulphur dioxide emissions are down to about 2.8 million tonnes.
We know that Canadian actions alone cannot solve the acid rain problem. For this reason we have been pressing the U.S. administration to negotiate a bilateral accord with specific emission control targets and schedules to reduce the transboundary flow of acid rain pollutants to acceptable levels. Canada's objective is based on sound scientific information and existing principles and obligations under international law. Canada recognizes that how the United States goes about reducing its transboundary pollution flow to 2 million tonnes is its business. Canada's legitimate interest is in the extent to which transboundary pollution flows are and will be reduced. Canada will judge all U.S. initiatives against this yardstick.
1 welcome the opportunity to put on the record once again the Government's outstanding achievement in having federal-provincial agreements now in place in order to accomplish our goals in the reduction of sulphur emissions.
